subsubtopic: PRIME MINISTER'S MEETING WITH PRESIDENT CARTER-DISCUSSION OF ALASKA HIGHWAY PIPELINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. There is real apprehension in this country that, after great expectations for Canada's economy as a whole, the Alaskan pipeline project is a dead duck and that we have all been led up the garden path, perhaps by the Americans or perhaps by our own government which should have known better.
MS)
The Prime Minister is going to Washington to have discussions with President Carter. On the assumption that this is not merely a public relations exercise, may I ask the Prime Minister if the pipeline project is on the agenda and, if so, what presentation will the Prime Minister make to the President about it?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF HUDSON'S BAY BY THOMSON INTERESTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister also. It arises from the announcement today indicating that the Thomson interests are seeking to secure control of the Hudson's Bay Company, which only recently acquired control of Simpsons and Zeller's.
In view of the fact that last January the assistant deputy minister of consumer and corporate affairs, who is also in charge of the combines investigation and research branch of that department, said that the takeover by the Hudson's Bay Company of Simpsons was against the public interest because it would mean department stores sales would be 35 per cent under the control of this company-and if we include Simp-sons-Sears, it would be 60 per cent-will the Prime Minister indicate when we can expect the competition legislation which the government has repeatedly told us it intends to introduce?
I refer particularly to last Tuesday, when the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said that instead of a fair prices commission, the federal government's preference was proper competition legislation. Can we expect that legislation during this session and, if not, what action does the government propose to take in light of this announcement by the Thomson interests?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, there is in fact combines legislation

existing now and there is, as he mentioned, a director of investigations and research under that act, a combines commissioner.
I again talked with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs this morning, and because of the very magnitude of that proposed takeover, the facts are being looked at by the director of investigations.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF HUDSON'S BAY BY THOMSON INTERESTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last January, in a speech which the director of investigations made to the Canadian Club in Montreal, he said that the present combines legislation was not adequate to cope with the takeover of Simpsons by Hudson's Bay.
In view of this very much larger takeover, I would ask the Prime Minister whether he would be prepared to follow the example of Premier Bennett of British Columbia, who persuaded the Canadian Pacific Railways to put off its acquisition of MacMillan Bloedel until such time as effective legislation could be put in place by parliament.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure 1 follow the hon. member in his suggestion that Premier Bennett was justified in suggesting that one Canadian company would not be able to take over another Canadian company. I am surprised that the hon. member is supporting the attitude of the provincial premier.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the right hon. Prime Minister. On February 14, the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced outside this House that agreement had been reached on Atlantic coast fisheries and boundary disputes, and that two treaties-one on the third party settlement of the boundary and the other on fisheries arrangements-will be completed and ready for signature by the beginning of March.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. On February 13, in answer to a question put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning a possible claim by the United States to Canadian territorial waters, he undertook to provide me with information in this regard, which he has done in a letter addressed to me dated February 22. It confirms my worst fears by informing me that the United States has formally claimed continental shelf and fisheries jurisdiction in the Beaufort Sea up to an equidistant line which lies east of the 141st meridian, an area of approximately 6,000 square nautical miles.
In his visit to Washington, can the Prime Minister assure the House that he will take a firm stand on informing the

March 2, 1979

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON TERRITORIAL BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course Canada will not relinquish sovereignty over any of its waters. I can say that to the House and I can say that to the President.
The whole question is, where does Canada's sovereignty lie and where does the boundary lie? As the hon. member knows, or should know, this is the whole subject of negotiation. We have made claim over waters that the United States say is an infringement of their sovereignty. The President can tell me the same thing: you must not take our sovereign waters.
The whole matter is one of discussing and deciding where the line lies. That is the object of the negotiations and that will perhaps be the eventual object of arbitration.

speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Since Canada has always operated under the sector theory, the 141st meridian, therefore, would be the established boundary of Canada's territorial waters.
Can the Prime Minister assure us that the Canadian government is taking that stance; that it is insisting upon the application of the sector theory, and that the 141st meridian is the established rigid boundary of Canada's territorial waters in that area of the country?

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON TERRITORIAL BOUNDARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sector theory is the one which gives us the broadest scope of sovereignty. It is, of course, the one we are pushing for and prefer, but it is not the one which is accepted in international law or by the United States.
It would be very nice to go up to the North Pole and say that part of the North Pole is ours, but it would be another thing to get the rest of the world to admit that claim. The hon. member knows the difficulties when there are competing claims by different countries. You have to resolve those claims by negotiation, as we have been successful in doing on the east coast and as we hope to be successful in doing elsewhere. Failing that, we will use the other means at our disposal under international law.

subtopic: PROBLEMS OF INDEPENDENT FUEL OIL DISTRIBUTORS- MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two problems with respect to the shortage of stove oil and furnace oil in Quebec. The first problem, and the No. 1 priority of the government, is to ensure consumers of stove oil and fuel oil that they will be looked after.
The government has made a number of efforts to ensure that federal arms, such as the Department of National Defence, for instance, have shipped stove oil from the special reserve in Newfoundland into the Quebec market.
Similarly, the Minister of Transport has made special efforts to get the air carriers of Canada to switch fuels temporarily so that more kerosene will be made available to consumers of stove oil in the province of Quebec. I believe that these methods, along with certain other reallocations on the part of eastern refiners to the Quebec market, have helped the situation.
The second problem the hon. member raises is the question of allocation and the position of the independents. We have made every effort to get the co-operation of the refiners to make a fair distribution. I am not satisfied as yet that that fair distribution has been obtained. We have advised the refiners that we have some evidence which indicates they are taking advantage of the situation. I can tell the hon. member that as a result of that evidence I have issued instructions to my department that I want an audit made and an investigation into certain practices in the province of Quebec.

PROPOSED CUTBACK IN IMPORTS-EFFECT OF IEA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In 1974, Canada became one of the signatory countries to the International Energy Agency agreement. One of the clauses in that agreement provided that Canada would reduce its consumption of petroleum products if oil exports from certain sources fell below a certain figure.
Would the minister advise us how Canada proposes to cut back its imports by 5 per cent under that agreement as announced this morning?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: PROPOSED CUTBACK IN IMPORTS-EFFECT OF IEA AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The governing board of the International Energy Agency met in Paris yesterday and reached a decision to work collectively to reduce world oil demand by two million barrels a day, roughly 5 per cent of the consumption by International Energy Agency countries. The purpose of this decision was to move demand and supply into balance and reduce pressure on prices, particularly spot prices.
As to the methods to be used by these countries operating separately and in addition to obligations under the emergency oil sharing agreement, there are a variety of procedures. They include demand restraint where it would not impair economic activity, the substitution of other fuels for oil where that might work, and increases in indigenous production. The hon. member will recognize that the last named method is one which Canada has already used. By virtue of the swapping arrangements we have been able to manage our resources in such a way that there was reserve capacity, and that reserve has been moved to the east coast. So Canada is already performing in accordance with the undertakings which other countries have assumed.

They have attempted to emasculate the Human Rights Act which I know the Prime Minister wants. What is going on here? When we passed this legislation, I thought it would not be selective, but it seems that this government is attempting to make it selective. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I discussed the matter a few days ago with the Minister of Justice. I have not discussed it with him since and I do not know what developments have taken place with regard to the position taken by the commissioner and the fact that some legislation and some actions are before the courts.
I knew that the issue was that the commission should wait to see what the courts were deciding in this particular case. I believe that would be the position of the hon. member, too. The law must prevail. This is a matter for the courts to decide, and I believe that was the situation a few days ago. I do not know what has come out of that court action since.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am extremely disappointed and very surprised at the Prime Minister's answer, because he too is going along with selectivity in the process. I find that to be very obnoxious. On the order paper now there is a bill which contains the following clause:
Nothing in this act shall be construed as limiting the application of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
The Prime Minister knows that when I am serious, I am serious. I am not going to get smart with him. Would he see to it, in the last days of this parliament, that any legislation which is introduced will take account of the clause to which I have referred? Perhaps it is necessary that such a clause be included in all legislation. Failing that, we will have legislation which will be nothing but a sham and a fraud; we will have reduced the commissioner to the level of someone who has no power whatsoever.

Mr. Speaker, in spite of the hon. member's plea to be taken seriously, I am afraid that the last part of his question shows that he is not very serious. This House debated that bill at great length. It was presented in utmost earnest by the government. We chose to head the commission with an honourable and respected member of the hon. member's party.
But look at what you are doing to him.
The law is taking its course. Surely the hon. member is not asking the government to phone a judge to tell him to stand aside in this case.
I am saying that there should be no exceptions, and the Prime Minister has not answered my question. That is a sham and a fraud.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
that Bill C-43, to amend the Judges Act, to amend an act to amend the Judges Act and to amend certain other acts in respect of the reconstitution in the courts of New Brunswick, Alberta and Saskatchewan, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to thank the opposition parties for their co-operation in the consideration of this bill, Bill C-43. I hope that once we have heard from all parties on this bill we will get agreement to pass this bill through the three stages today in the House.
In effect, this bill, while urgent and extremely useful for a few provinces in particular, is one that should not give rise to long debates or arguments and differences of view on what it tries to achieve. The bill tries to accomplish two purposes. First, it would give effect to a restructuring of the courts systems in the provinces of New Brunswick and Alberta and a proposed restructuring in the province of Saskatchewan.

Second, the bill would replenish the pool of judicial salaries provided for appointments to provincial superior, county and district courts over and above fixed complements.
The restructuring of the courts systems in the three provinces I have mentioned requires amendments to the Judges Act and a number of other statutes so that the restructuring can be given full effect. As is well known by hon. members, the provinces have full jurisdiction to determine what courts they will have. Alberta and New Brunswick have already exercised their jurisdiction in this respect and Saskatchewan is in the process of doing so.
If the House were to agree to proceed to the committee stage, I have an amendment to clause 12 which I will move at that time. I understand that that proposed amendment has been circulated to the opposition parties and they have it in their hands at present. It would be made as a result of a request made by the attorney general of New Brunswick, a request which I have just received today. The amendment would provide that the provisions relating to New Brunswick will come into force on proclamation, as opposed to July 1, 1979, as presently provided. The original provision in the bill for New Brunswick was that it should come into force in that province on July 1, 1979, but the attorney general of that province has just written me saying that they did not think they would be able to put it into effect on July 1 and would like it to be delayed and put into force on proclamation. Their expectation is that their legislation would be in operation on September 1.

Would the minister permit a question at this point? He said that in committee he would move an amendment to clause 12. There is no clause 12 in the reprint of the bill, although there was one in the previous printing. I assume he proposes to move an amendment to clause 11.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Yes, I quite agree, Mr. Speaker; the amendment is to clause 11.
As I said, the government of New Brunswick intends to pass legislation changing the effective date of the merger of the courts from July 1 to September 1, and this amendment is made at their request to facilitate their change in plans.
The second purpose of the bill is the restoration to full strength of the pool of additional judges, provisions first enacted by parliament in 1973. It is basically a housekeeping matter necessitated by the fact that 17 judicial appointments have been made and charged, so to speak, to the pool since it was last replenished by parliament in 1976. The proposal is to have the Judges Act itself indicate clearly the number of judges comprising each court and therefore the exact number of salaries approved by parliament, and at the same time bring the pool up to its full complement of 34 judicial salaries, plus another 15 for unified family courts, so that further appointments that are required can be made without the immediate necessity of amending the Judges Act.
In closing, I would again like to thank the opposition parties for their agreement to, and support of, this measure.
March 2, 1979

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde). We have had several bills. That is not due to his error because like everyone else he has to rely on other people, and I will not make anything of that. But finally we have received the right version.
I can incorporate in my remarks what the minister has said about that bill, that is that the main purpose of the bill is to amalgamate the district courts of Saskatchewan, Alberta and New Brunswick with the high trial court, which in Alberta would mean the amalgamation of the district court of Alberta with the Supreme Court trial division, which henceforth will be known as the Queen's Bench, and in Saskatchewan it would amalgamate the district court of Saskatchewan with their Queen's Bench, which is their trial court. The same goes for New Brunswick. In the course of amalgamation, the district courts will disappear.
I want to emphasize that district court judges receive less remuneration than high court trial judges of the provinces. The question of salary is mentioned in the bill; it brings the salaries of district court judges up to the level of the new positions they will hold because of the amalgamation of the two courts. There is no suggestion in the bill that the salaries of judges are being increased. When the district court judges move into their new positions and are faced with the new responsibilities of the high court trial divisions of the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and New Brunswick, then of course they would receive fair remuneration as set by law and parliament.
I should like to digress somewhat, or as they say in the army, "As you were".
At ease!

Right on. As was pointed out by the Minister of Justice, parliament previously set up a pool of salaries in reference to new appointments. Rather than coming to parliament each time a new appointment is necessary, particularly when parliament is busy dealing with complex matters, the pool of salaries is available. For example, if a provincial attorney general hears from the trial division chief justice and the Court of Appeal chief justice of his province that extra judges are needed to carry the workload, an appointment is made and a salary is paid out of that pool equivalent to the salary paid to judges as set out by parliament in the last bill before it. Of course, we endorse that pool.
If I might again digress for a few moments, I should like to indicate that we are dealing with an institution when we are dealing with the judiciary which sometimes receives criticism because of its independence. Judges must have a degree of independence because they are separate and apart, under our democratic system, from the legislative processes of parliament. Often they are criticized because of the degree of independence and the positions they take in administering justice. To put it in layman's language, they are criticized
Judges Act
because of the roles they play in trying civil matters and indeed very difficult criminal matters. Of course, they are not able to answer such criticism.
I know I speak for the Minister of Justice when I indicate in a non-partisan manner that on the whole Canada has a very fine judiciary. Of course, I am not speaking for everyone and, as I say, I am not speaking in a partisan manner. I am speaking from the point of view of all parties working together and the liaison existing among the various provincial bar associations and the Canadian Bar Association. In the last 10 or 15 years, the judiciary has been able to obtain people from various law firms or those who were deans of colleges. The judiciary has attracted a calibre of men who have the capacity to make decisions and administer justice. Canadians feel that this calibre of men is necessary.
I should like to take a moment to pay tribute to a man in my own province who has retired as chief justice of the province of Alberta. I am referring to Chief Justice J. Valentine Milvain who was appointed to the Supreme Court trial division of Alberta Dy the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). After serving some time on that bench with distinction, Mr. Milvain was appointed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government to chief justice of the province of Alberta. In drawing that analogy and in paying this gentleman a great compliment, I have shown that we have endeavoured to move along the road away from the narrow, partisan belief that only people of certain political stripes, if that certain political party is in power, get the nod and receive an appointment to the bench. We have not gone as far as we can in that direction, but it is a step in the right direction.
I might say that I knew Chief Justice Valentine Milvain when he was practising as a lawyer and before he went on the bench. He was always very courteous. After he received his appointment, he was always very discreet, polite, knowledgeable, learned and was quite a humanist. Above all, he had a sense of humour. For example, when a most difficult trial was taking place before him with questions being put and answers being given, as we have witnessed from time to time during oral question period, sometimes the atmosphere became somewhat inflammatory. He was a judge with a sense of humour and he would bring the lawyers either for the defence or the Crown, or for the plaintiff or the defendant, back to the degree of reasonable sanity which is necessary in the administration of justice. I know I speak for members of the House when I wish Chief Justice Val Milvain well in his retirement. I can say that Alberta is sorry to see this man being forced into retirement because of his age. I only mention this in passing because I feel the gentleman is symbolic of the types of people who are being attracted to the judiciary.
Traditionally bills respecting salary increases are brought before parliament for approval. Judges are not overpaid by any means. Many of them give up law practices in which they would make twice as much money as they make on the bench. I could name many such judges but I will not. We must exercise care to see that these men and women receive the necessary compensation to exercise the degree of independence

March 2, 1979
Judges Act
and the degree of integrity demanded of them. Not only must they remain aloof in their jobs; they must keep their powers separate and apart from the other processes of democracy.
Also they must keep their economic affairs separate and apart because of their position. Most of them are not able to make investments in corporations A and B because corporations A and B come before them tomorrow in a law suit. In analysing the compensation paid to judges, we must take a hard look at the position they hold in society. Because they are judges, they are judging people and corporations. They are judging morals and the law, which flow from the morals set by the Criminal Code. They must remain aloof from any outside influence which would suggest any indiscretion on their part in making decisions. On the whole, I think I can safely say, after looking over the judiciary, that that has been accomplished.
I should like to say a few words in reference to the amalgamation of the courts. In my early years I had the privilege of practising in the province of Saskatchewan, and later I went to the province of Alberta. When it came to the high court, one was called the Queen's Bench and the other was called the Supreme Court trial court. Although they were named differently, they were almost identical.
This bill is not being produced today because the government decided to amalgamate the courts and the Minister of Justice accepted that direction, but rather because the federal government has received a mandate or a direction from the provincial governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick.
In our busy society of today, with an increase in population and because of the heavy court backlog in some provinces, it has become necessary to increase the number of judges. It was felt that in some districts the district court judges had the capacity to do more work and to take on more responsibility. The district courts in Saskatchewan and Alberta have pretty well the same jurisdiction. They deal with mechanics' lien act cases and with matters involving amounts up to $2,500, although that has fluctuated up to $3,500 in one province. Under the Criminal Code these courts deal with speedy trials when an accused elects to do without a jury. Sometimes they involve pleas of guilty or the hearing of a few witnesses. In these cases the accused elect to have a speedy trial and go before the district court judge. This relieves the pressure of a large number of trials in the high court.
District courts also deal with an important part of criminal law, trials de novo, and I want to say something about this. Under the code offences which are not indictable, generally not serious offences, are summary conviction offences and are tried by the provincial court judges. They used to be called magistrates in police courts, but they changed the name because it was felt the judges were too close to the police. I do not know whether by changing the name they altered the atmosphere, but one thing I do know is that they now call them provincial judges and they deal with summary conviction cases.
If a person found guilty in such a court feels aggrieved, or on the other hand if the Crown thinks an individual was wrongly acquitted, the case can then go before a district judge by way of a trial de novo. Up until two years ago that meant a district court judge would re-try the case by hearing witnesses for the Crown and for the defence, and most of the time they were the same witnesses. Two years ago that was changed so that the district court judge could use discretion as to whether there would be a full trial or just a review of the matter through the record.
I pointed out at the time the amendment was made that every district court judge enjoying that discretion would almost always elect to proceed by way of a review of the record because it is much easier and much simpler. As the Minister of Justice and other lawyers present who have had this experience are aware, there is no appeal from a wrong finding of fact, only an appeal on a question of law. In most cases of summary conviction offences there is very little law involved so appeals are not very successful under this new method. I opposed this at the time and I still oppose it because, while there has been an improvement in the last few years, during the period when these courts were known as police courts the Crown was always very close to the police and it was very difficult to obtain what would appear to be-and sometimes it was more than that-an impartial trial. Once you got the case out of that atmosphere and into the district court, you got a more fair and better trial.
I would presume that when the two courts are united the same situation will occur. There will no longer be a trial de novo as such but rather a review of the evidence. As there is no appeal possible on the law it will make a sham of the right of appeal in this regard.
I am concerned about another thing, and this is not by way of criticizing the minister or his bill. This is a matter really involving the provinces. I refer to the question of estates. In the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan the district courts administer estates in the right to grant probate. Just to put it simply, and application for probate is generally made by a solicitor, setting out the assets with affidavits of witnesses proving the will and so on. This is laid before the judge and there is no application as such. These documents are looked at and examined in an administrative fashion. If there does not appear to be any mathematical error or question about the full disclosure of children, or something of that nature, probate is automatically granted. This surrogate court work really falls within the jurisdiction of provinces rather than the federal government.
For a number of years district court judges have received extra salaries from the provinces over and above what they were paid by the federal government for doing this surrogate court work. I do not know what the Supreme Court trial judges who took on that job before amalgamation are going to say about becoming local administrators of estates.
Let me make a suggestion to the Minister of Justice through you, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps he could pass this on when he is writing the attorneys general of those provinces. This work

March 2, 1979

could be given to somebody who is on the provincial staffs taking these applications in the courts, such as a master in chambers, or something like that. I cannot believe that with the extensive work now being done by the high court trial judges in Saskatchewan, Alberta and New Brunswick-and I understand Ontario is to be phased in-they should be involved in this administrative work. This administration work does take some time, but it does not require the services of anyone other than an efficient clerk. In fact, let me make a confession on behalf of lawyers. I would say that 90 per cent of estates that go through a law firm are handled by experienced secretaries. The lawyer looks at the work to make sure it is all right, puts on his signature and it goes to the court house. I would not like to go that far in respect of mortgages, but I have been lucky to have had the same secretary for almost as long as I have practised and I think she knows more than a lot of lawyers. She does an excellent job. I am sure that if I did it I would probably make a mathematical error. The point I am making is that this is straight administrative work. I suggest that is one matter that could be removed from the jurisdiction of the high courts. Of course, that is up to the provinces.
Having said that, let me end on this note. On behalf of my party I have agreed that this bill should be the subject of a short debate on second reading, which is now taking place, and then referred to the committee of the whole House. There is apparently no contention, so it possibly could be given third reading today. I hope my learned counsel to the left will go along with that in his usual good humour. If the bill is referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, along with the referendum bill and the estimates, I do not think it will see the light of day before we have a new government; therefore, I suggest it should go to the committee of the whole. There should be no discussion and it ought to go through in a few minutes.
I am willing now to sit down and listen to the leading counsel in the House, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

Mr. Speaker, I have had some delightful and some embarrassing introductions in my day, but I do not know what I can say in reply, to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), except that I am happy to participate for a few minutes in the debate on Bill C-43.
The motion you put at the beginning of this debate, Mr. Speaker, called for the reference of this bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I am happy to indicate to you that we are prepared to go along with the request of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) and the agreement expressed by the hon. member for Calgary North. I agree that when it comes time to give second reading to this bill the motion should be amended so that the bill will go to a committee of the whole House.

speechtext:
I heard the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), but the minister
Judges Act
did not give an indication that he was ready to proceed. If he is we will modify the motion, with the consent of the House, and go in to committee of the whole.

I believe you will find, Mr. Speaker, that although the Minister of Justice did not say that when he presented the motion, he did say it in the course of his remarks. I think you will find that there is agreement. We join in that agreement, partly for the reason just given by the hon. member for Calgary North, namely that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs is overloaded with work, and partly because the matters contained in Bill C-43 are routine. They are quite straight forward and I see no reason why we cannot deal with them today in committee of the whole.
I hope that the government House leader will be made aware of our co-operation in this respect and that the favour will be returned on occasion. After all, there are some pieces of legislation which we on this side of the House would like to put through quickly. Lor example, in the field of veterans affairs, just as we are ready today to put this bill through all stages, we would hope that the government would give us a chance to put some veterans legislation through all stages before this session comes to an end.
As the two previous speakers have pointed out, there are two main provisions in this bill. On the one hand it increases the number of judges which can be appointed to the courts at various levels to cope with the workload facing our courts; on the other hand it provides for the amalgamation of certain courts in Alberta, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick. I think it is relevant to note, particularly in the latter case, that we are simply responding to requests from the various provinces which are affected, and that it is appropriate for us to see that this legislation does not get bogged down.
My friend from Calgary North said some nice things about the judiciary. I do not intend to expand on the subject at length, but I am happy to confirm what he said. In fact, I can say that in my experience in this House I have seen some very partisan members of parliament get appointed to the bench, and I have always been amazed at the metamorphosis that takes place, almost overnight, once they get into the responsible position of being on the bench. They seem quickly to develop a capacity for fairness and impartiality, and I hope that it will continue that way. I join with my friend in the tribute which he paid to our Canadian judiciary.
My hon. friend also had something to say about the salaries of judges, although there is no provision in this bill to increase those salaries. That brings me to something which I would like to say about the explanatory notes in the bill as it is now before us. The hon. member for Calgary North made the point with regard to the salaries of judges that many lawyers could make more money staying in their law practices than they can by taking a position on the bench. That, of course, is their decision. I believe that many of them welcome the chance to be appointed to the bench because of the contribution which they can make and because of the prestige of the position. In other words, the salary is not everything.

It is like members of parliament.

That is right; the salary is not everything in either case. Since at the present time restraint is being preached, especially to the little people, I think that it would have been a gross error for the government to ask us to include salary increases for the judges in passing this bill. As a matter of fact, if that had happened there would not be consent to put it through all stages at this time.
I hope I am not saying anything out of order or talking out of school when I say that this matter has been discussed. Indeed, there is evidence of it in the two printings of this bill. Mr. Speaker, I am the last one who would want to raise a point of order with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but since he is embarking on this question of the two printings of the bill, I would like to inform the House-although, more properly, it should probably come from the Chair-that the bill to which the Speaker gave first reading in this House is the bill that is before us today.
I understand that when the bill was sent to printing an error was made. The printer used the wrong plates and, as a result, a bill was distributed which was not the bill to which the speaker actually gave first reading. In that sense, the bill with the salary clause, which the hon. member has in his hands, never existed before the House as such. It is a non-existent bill.

I am quite happy to accept that explanation, Mr. Speaker. I was not raising a point of order or alleging that a non-existent bill is before the House. I accept the fact that the bill before us is the one which has "reprint" at the top.
The point I was trying to make is that obviously there had been some consideration in this regard. After all, this nonexistent bill does exist, if I may speak in existential rather than legal terms. I am glad that any suggestion of salary increase has disappeared from the various printings of the bill.
You can always send your salary back, Stanley. I have told you that for years. I will take care of the legal ramifications.
By the time I got through dealing with my friend, there would not be much money left to worry about.
That would relieve your anxiety.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: It would also relieve his pocket book!

I have found other and better ways to relieve that anxiety. I am glad that we are passing today the bill and not the explanatory notes. The Minister of Justice points out that it was the corrected form which was handed in for first reading, but if one goes through the bill and reads the explanatory notes, it is obvious that they were written with something else in mind, and when the bill got changed these explanatory notes were not changed.
As a matter of fact, this bothered me at the House leaders' meeting this morning when the question of going into committee of the whole on this bill was raised, because I was aware of the confusion created by the explanatory notes, and I therefore felt that the bill ought to go to the standing committee. Since then, after getting advice from certain learned counsel, I have examined the bill very carefully, and although, as I say, the explanatory notes lead to much confusion and make one wonder what is being explained, I do not find any trouble with the actual wording of the 11 clauses in the bill itself. Accordingly, we are prepared not only to give the bill second reading, but to agree that it be referred to a committee of the whole House.

Mr. Speaker, I see that there are a few minutes left before one o'clock. There are some things that I would like to say about the bill, most of which will be acceptable, but I may have one or two things to say which may not be quite so acceptable. Generally, I favour the bill for a number of reasons.
Approximately 25 years ago I was a bencher of the Law Society of Alberta. This particular issue involving the joinder of the two courts is a matter in which I was involved and on which I spoke at several meetings of the Alberta Bar Association. I think the judgment of the government with regard to carrying forward the submissions made by the government of Alberta is very wise. I believe I have also spoken on this matter in this House.
As a member of the bar who practised for a great many years in rural areas, I know there was often a feeling among many people that an inferior type of justice was dispensed at the district court level. I know that many members of the district court, which has become the court of Queen's Bench in Alberta, were fine people, and I subscribe to the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) as to the quality of the bench. There was one judge whom we used to call "the judge of necessity," because there is an ancient maxim that necessity knows no law. He was one of the exceptions, however.
There was a feeling among many people that there was a choice between going to district court or to Supreme Court, but actually this is dictated by the amount of the claim in a suit for damages.
Because of the inequality that exists in the justice dispensed by the different courts, I think the move to amend the act is

March 2, 1979

commendable and should have been done long ago. I am happy to lend my support to the bill, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to subscribe as well to the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North about former Chief Justice Mil-vain, who is a very old friend of mine. We served together as benchers. He has followed a great tradition in the province of Alberta.
When I come to write my memoirs I will include the fact that the late Prime Minister Pearson did me the honour of inviting me to go to the bench. I declined because at the time 1 thought I had a more useful role to perform here, although I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) smilingly queries that.
I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that there are a number of statutes under which the federal government has the right to initiate proceedings, one being the Official Secrets Act. One of the shocking things about it, however, is the matter of selection of judges to try a case.
In the recent Treu case there was a very serious, formidable charge and the minister of justice of the day, on the advice of his officials-I absolve the present Minister of Justice entirely as he was not involved-saw fit to direct that the party be tried before a provincial judge. I have nothing against the quality of provincial judges, Mr. Speaker, but I am given to understand that the judge in question had just recently been appointed. The charge was laid on the instructions of the minister of justice who, as attorney general, exercises a judicial function under the Official Secrets Act. When the question whether a charge should be laid arises, then in theory the minister of justice is no longer a politician but has to exercise a judicial function.
Because of the formidable character of this act, because of the severe penalties involved, because of the type of procedure that might well be involved in carrying on proceedings, no charge can be made until the minister of justice has an opportunity to survey the facts and decide, on the advice of senior officials and security people, whether a charge should be laid and, if so, what kind of charge. The charge can be laid as an indictable offence with the potential of a very severe penalty, or as a summary offence with the potential of a fine.
In the case in question, the minister of justice, no doubt on the advice of his officials, saw fit to instruct that the charge be laid as an indictable offence to be heard before a provincial court judge who, it happened, had limited experience. I do not question the capacity of the judge; I understand he had been a Crown prosecutor shortly before his appointment. My view is that a minister of justice, theoretically standing apart from his colleagues in the political sense and making that kind of decision, should exercise a great deal more care than did the then minister of justice in the case of Peter Treu.
The minister has said that a group of departmental officials is reviewing this act. I hope they will keep in mind that most judges in this country and in the United Kingdom who have had occasion to try cases involving the Official Secrets Act have not only tried the people appearing before them but have
Judges Act
tried the act and found it guilty. Most have held that the act requires very severe changes to be made to it.
I hope that the minister, in the time that elapses before this parliament comes to a conclusion, or whoever may follow him as minister of justice, will take it as a prior order of business that not only should there be an examination of the act by departmental officials, but also by a committee of parliament. The act does not deserve to survive in its present form. This is tremendously important, Mr. Speaker.
I am one of the few people outside those involved in the Treu case who know the facts. I was co-counsel for Dr. Treu and had access to information. I looked at the evidence and I thoroughly agree with the fine judgment of the three judges of the Quebec Court of Appeal. I think anyone who reads the reasons for judgment carefully will agree that there are grave dangers in allowing that act to be used, for charges to be laid under the conditions which existed in the case of Dr. Treu, and for his being charged before a provincial judge.
I am fully convinced that once there had been a fruitless investigation leading to the expenditure of several hundreds of thousands of dollars, Dr. Treu stood as a symbol of the stupidity and bumbling involved. I do not suggest this occurred at the ministerial level. I do not believe that the former minister is that kind of man. But a decision was made at some place to see that this man was put out of the way for a while. That is the grave danger which exists and it points out the necessity for the government to be careful in the appointments that are made and in the way its powers are used to initiate proceedings involving statutes such as the Official Secrets Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, what I am about to say I could have said on the second reading debate before lunch, but I wanted to add to the assurance given to the Minister of Justice that it was our intention to deal with this bill expeditiously and thought I would add to that assurance by speaking first on the consideration of clause 1.
One might wonder why a lawyer from Ontario who is a member of the House of Commons would speak with regard to the amalgamation of federal trial courts in the provinces of Alberta, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan. However, the subject matter is really important. The bill is important because of the provinces involved, but it is equally important and applicable to my own province of Ontario-and I will deal further with that aspect in a few moments.
My hon. friend from Peace River said something modestly or else my hearing was modest; if he did not say it, it should have been said. That is that the proposal set out in this piece of legislation was put forward by him when he was a bencher of the Law Society of Alberta some 25 years ago because it has been the quest of those interested in judicial matters to bring some order into and continue the development of order in the legal system.
What this bill really provides is that the trial division of what I would call the high court in the province of Ontario, the trial division in those three provinces, would be amalgamated with the district court, not necessarily by an increase in the number of judges, though there would certainly be an increase paid generally for judges' salaries. I think the objective is worth while and I commend the minister for bringing this measure forward.
I said this was important to me, to the bench and to the bar in the province of Ontario and I want to explain that statement to the minister. We have in this province two levels of courts, three if you count the small claims court and four if you count the provincial court. But with federally appointed judges there are two levels of trial courts, the High Court of Justice trial division and the county and district courts. The history and evolution of our society, increasing the monetary jurisdiction and increasing the subject matter jurisdiction of the courts, have imposed upon the county and district courts of Ontario and upon the judges of those courts a tremendous burden by way of extra workload. Therefore, I hope that through the message of this bill the attorney general of Ontario will cause
[The Chairman.]
to be reviewed once again the proposals of the report of the Law Reform Commission of Ontario issued in 1973, a really monumental work with respect to the administration of justice within the province.
A proposal was presented to that very distinguished commission by the County and District Court Judges Association. The proposal was considered by the commission. It asked for precisely the same kind of thing which is now granted by this bill to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and New Brunswick. In its proposal the County and District Court Judges Association laid out what a judicial system is supposed to do in society. I am reading from page 92 of the report as follows:
Modern society requires a judicial system which, without being exhaustive, possesses the following characteristics: (1) Reasonable expedition in the determination of litigants' disputes, (2) Economy for both the litigants and society, (3) Accessibility to all members of society irrespective of their means or station in life, (4) Volume-handling ability to accommodate the litigation explosion corresponding, not only with increased population, but also with increased accessibility and justiciability of new grievances, (5) Comprehensibility of the system to the public for whose needs it exists and (6) "Justice" of the decisions in the sense of confidence among all members and sectors of society in the competence of the decision-makers and quality of their decisions.
I think those are not bad criteria for anyone to consider in terms of what ought to motivate one when one is considering the construction of a judicial system. I point out that the judges were supported by the Ontario Sheriffs' and Court Registrars' Association, which is involved closely with the dispensation of justice and legal services to the citizens of the province of Ontario, in that that association advocated the union of the Supreme Court of Ontario trial division and the county and district courts of the province of Ontario into one superior court for the purposes of hearing trials, and I will deal with how that term specifically arose.
It is a matter of some misfortune and regret that while the government of Ontario adopted a large number of the administrative procedures which were laid out in that excellent, monumental and exhaustive report, for some reason which I cannot discern the government of Ontario chose not to adopt this plan with respect to the union of the courts. I do not say that in criticism. I know there was great pressure from the judges of the high court of the province of Ontario not to have this done, for reasons with which I respectfully dissent and disagree. However, it did not happen in the province of Ontario.
We are wiser in Saskatchewan and Alberta.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Calgary North says they are wiser in Saskatchewan and Alberta, and that may very well be, I do not know. I would not want to admit that today. It is Friday afternoon and I will not argue very strenuously with the hon. member on that point.
Because finding candidates for the bench is important, I want to let the Minister of Justice know that there was a memorandum of dissent and explanation filed by a member of the Law Reform Commission who at one time was a member of this House. The Hon. Richard Albert Bell, P.C., Q.C., was
March 2, 1979

a member of the Elouse of Commons from 1957 until 1968 with one period of time out of the House while he returned to the practice of law. I willingly tell my friends in this House that that gentleman happens to be the senior partner of the law firm with which I am associated. I feel it would be inappropriate for me not to say that, having regard to the provisions of Bill C-6 which we might get to at some stage.
That dissenting view which, unfortunately, was not accepted, did involve the amalgamation of the trial division of the high court and the county and district courts, but it did something else too. The memorandum of dissent and explanation also advocated that for judicial purposes the province of Ontario should be divided up into a number of judicial districts so that judges would then be judges having the same jurisdiction. Mr. Bell proposed that they be called judges of the superior court and that they not have to move around to any great extent, which is quite important in terms of the life of a judge. The memorandum of dissent and explanation advocated within each of those districts a small hierarchy so that there could be a president or a chief judge within each of those districts.
That is important to the Minister of Justice because he is responsible for making recommendations, too, and joins his colleagues in cabinet in the decision-making process to decide who among the barristers in a particular province will join the federally appointed court of that province. I have talked to people who have been invited but who have declined, and some do, as the minister knows. One of the reasons they decline is that if one is to follow the law of the province-and there is some doubt as to whether all our high court judges do in terms of residence-one must uproot one's family and move to Toronto. That may be a very happy thing for the hon. member for Rosedale but it is sometimes unhappy for the families of judges. Judges must leave the communities in which they have taken an active part for many years and hive themselves off in Osgoode Hall.
If the judges involved are trial judges, they devote the rest of their lives to travelling in the province of Ontario. That is a very happy thing when one does it under happy circumstances. It is not always the best thing, however, when it has to be considered among a host of other things one might do. I think the adoption of this proposal would make the profession of judge one which would be easier to consider for highly qualified lawyers. That is one of the reasons it was regretted by me and by Mr. Bell that the commission did not see fit to adopt that proposal. It is very extensive and I commend its reading to the Minister of Justice.
There was one other important aspect. Despite the work of chief judges at all levels, but particularly at the levels about which we are talking, justice has been slow. Some of that slowness is to be blamed on the system, particularly on the perambulations of judges across the province of Ontario-and, I suspect, in other provinces as well-because of the necessity to accommodate the public and the legal profession. I would be the last to say that a great deal of the blame does not lie with
Judges Act
the legal profession, which has not been as expeditious as it might.
I think it is important that we look at the formation of the court, its functions and its administration from the point of view not necessarily of the judges or their convenience or of lawyers or their convenience but, rather, from the point of view of the public and the convenience of the public. I commend that to the Minister of Justice.
I am aware of constitutional problems with regard to the administration of justice, but I cannot help but feel that with the prestige of the Minister of Justice there might be some way by which this matter could be reawakened.
A constituent of mine, a Mrs. Mary Herron-who was in this chamber just before two o'clock, as a matter of fact, as guest of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris-from the community of Glencairn in the new city of Kanata, and who happens to be a nurse at the Civic hospital, said something to me when we were discussing the subject matter of the bill before us today, something which I think is important. She said "slow justice is not justice". I think that is a good phrase for all of us to remember, and it falls on the Minister of Justice in his capacity as Attorney General of Canada to look at procedures by which not only administrations improve but justice within a province is improved.
I want to turn to one other aspect. I said that the high court judges of the province of Ontario were not happy with the proposal of district courts and in fact spoke against it at the commission hearings. They said they would be abandoning the collegiality of Osgoode Hall. There is a certain collegiality at Osgoode Hall which would be lost, they said.
I suppose there are ways that could be remedied for those high court judges. I am sure that opinion is one they honestly hold, but what has happened and what can happen-and this is something which 1 think one should always guard against- is that the system and the judges within the system can lose their sense of collegiality with the community. I suggest to you, sir, that moving the courts into the community to a greater extent and amalgamating the jurisdictions could accomplish great things.
While the Minister of Justice is in the committee I want to turn to one other matter which was raised by the hon. member for Peace River, and I will do it briefly. It is very important when we consider the position of the Minister of Justice that we realize he is also a judicial officer, as the hon. member for Peace River said. There is built into our system a potential conflict of interest. Not only can the person who occupies the position of minister of justice find himself in a conflict of interest position, but there can appear to be a conflict of interest.
As we develop certain other things, we will have to consider the breaking up of the responsibilities of the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice is a member of the government who is responsible for the maintenance of the operation of his department. He could be a constitutional adviser to his

colleagues and to the Prime Minister. He has line responsibilities to the government which are very important. Those responsibilities might not coincide with his quasi-judicial function as Attorney General of Canada, and it is important, I think, that we consider the direction in which we are going.
The joint committee on statutory instruments is now considering a way of examining the regulatory power of governments as it falls from each statute, so that when there is a reference from this House to a particular standing committee of the House, there is a parallel reference of the power to make orders in council and statutory instruments to the joint committee to be considered. If this occurs, we will be calling upon the advice of the Attorney General, a judicial officer or quasi-judicial officer who, as the hon. member for Peace River would say, should stand apart from his colleagues in government. Not that a minister of justice personally would not attempt to stand apart, but that the Minister of Justice, now dubbed Attorney General, would be seen to stand apart from the line functions of the government.
This question was raised the other day when we were considering the application of the human rights code which this parliament passed with respect to immigration. The Minister of Justice is a colleague of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and as his colleague he has responsibility for the joint decision of the government, and all ministers are in that bag, even though from time to time one or two of them attempt to get out of it. There can arise out of that a case which could put the Minister of Justice in a difficult situation-

speechtext:
I thank my colleagues. I will speak only for a minute or two more.
The other area into which we are moving is the law with respect to freedom of information upon which decisions will have to be made and advice given to the executive, not on the basis of membership in the government but perhaps on the basis of advice to the government from an independent quasijudicial authority.
Finally, there is the matter which was raised by the hon. member for Calgary North which I think should be addressed, and that is the appointment of Her Majesty's judges. There has been a movement, which some see as a healthy movement, toward using consultation in areas outside the government. I consider it terribly unhealthy.
There are some in society who feel that perhaps the function of appointment, and therefore ultimately the responsibility for the appointment of Her Majesty's judges, should be undertak-

en by someone other than the Minister of Justice. I caution the minister that while it would be foolish for him not to consult the Canadian Bar Association and perhaps judges and the community, it would be equally foolish for him to give the impression in the excellent appointments that have been made-and, I am confident, will be made, regardless of what party forms the government-that the Minister of Justice be seen to have removed from himself or from the government of the day the ultimate responsibility for these appointments. Certainly he should consult, but not to such an extent that the appointment of Her Majesty's judges is seen to be taken away from the government of the day. I think it is one of the most important functions that a government performs.
I want to thank my colleagues in the House for indulging with me in the last two minutes or so and allowing me to complete those thoughts which I wanted to pass on today to the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief but I do think it is important to bring up a point which has always concerned me since I was elected to the House of Commons almost 11 years ago. Hon. members had the opportunity of considering that matter during the last session when we studied and passed Bill C-42 amending the Criminal Code and introduced a new section dealing with the language of the accused. Its purpose was, of course, to make our courts more humane, to ensure that, to the greatest possible extent at this juncture in Canadian history, the chosen official language of the accused is respected. So, the House proceeded to adopt those amendments thanks to which the accused, whether Francophone or Anglophone in Canada, no matter where he lives, now has a better chance of being heard and judged in the official language of his choice. However, I have always wondered why in an effort towards reform such as this, we did not go directly to the root of the problem.
I note that the bill before us today, Bill C-43, does not make any mention of being able to carry out a judge's duties in either of the two official languages of this country. Yet the hon. member who spoke before me quoted abundantly from a survey made in the province of Ontario and he said among other things that access of all members of society was an important factor in the delivery of legal services in this country.
So I am not trying to delay this bill unduly by raising this question. I represent in the parliament of Canada a group which is constantly concerned that justice be dealt fully for all Canadian citizens regardless of where they live in Canada. I am still curious and I would like to get an answer-how is it that in this proposed reform no mention is made of the languages of judges? I am not saying that judges in Canada, regardless of the province in which they reside, should be bilingual to qualify. Far from it, Mr. Chairman, that is not
March 2, 1979

what I am trying to get in a Canada which wants to remain united.
I believe the judiciary, starting with the judges themselves, should have at least that capacity. Individually, perhaps not, but generally I believe this country should guarantee that kind of representation. I note in the proposed constitutional reform, if one also refers to the constitution as it stands now, that it says a certain number of judges should originate from Quebec and other provinces. There is no question of language there as far as I know. I am not as learned as many members of this House who have a legal background, nevertheless I am talking for the man on the street, if I may put it that way. I am talking for the official language minorities, particularly French language minorities which always feel that their rights are being shortchanged. And in spite of the good will shown when Bill C-42 was considered, I believe progress is excessively slow in the provision of that fundamental justice in the delivery of legal services to all Canadians. Mr. Chairman, since I address myself to this particular aspect of the bill, the minister could perhaps take this opportunity to tell us what progress has been made since the passage last year of Bill C-42 concerning the language used by the accused with a view to ensuring greater justice throughout the country in the provision of French language services to the accused, or English language services if they live in Quebec of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would just like to say a few words in reply to the hon. member concerning the matter he has just raised.
First of all, I do not believe that the Judges Act as such would be the proper instrument to attack these problems. Other means have been found. As the hon. member stated, certain amendments have already been made to the Criminal Code to encourage the provinces to provide trials in one or the other of the official languages according to the choice of the accused as concerns criminal matters. Moreover, the hon. member is probably aware that during our constitutional discussions with the provinces concerning a human rights charter which would include linguistic rights, it was specifically provided that the provinces would be invited in this charter to guarantee to all their citizens the right to be heard in either official language, even in matters other than of a criminal nature. I am speaking about civil cases which come within provincial jurisdiction. I would also like to emphasize that enormous progress has been made concerning the ability of judges to speak and understand both official languages of Canada at the present time.
My department has financed a linguistic training program for judges which has been very useful. At the present time we can say, for instance, that on the whole the Supreme Court of Canada can operate very well in both official languages, that the Federal Court of Canada can also operate in both official languages, and I would like to mention simply the new chief justice of the provincial court, namely the Supreme Court of
Judges Act
Alberta, Mr. Justice Sinclair, who, thanks to these courses, can now speak perfectly in both languages and can express himself in a French which many French-speaking Canadians would envy.
Tremendous progress has been made, first by judges individually, second through amendments to the Criminal Code and, third, through the discussions taking place with the provinces concerning a linguistic rights charter. Finally, as concerns the appointment or the selection of judges, obviously the first criterion must be their juridical competence. Of course, if we need a judge for northern New Brunswick, we will try to appoint someone who is fluent in both official languages. The same situation prevails in some areas of Ontario and in the province of Quebec, of course, it is required by the constitution. The constitution does not require that every judge speak both languages but in Quebec you can be tried in the official language of your choice.
Now then, as concerns the specific question raised by the hon. member about the amendment made to the Criminal Code last year, there are continuous consultations with the provinces involved, particularly the province of Ontario, the province of New Brunswick, the province of Quebec, where it exists already, and I must say that remarkable progress has been made in Ontario in the last year. I cannot tell the hon. member exactly when those provinces will pass the proposed amendment. Recently we have had some administrative difficulties, perfectly understandable, having the staff required for the training courses at a given place, or a given date, so that the system may really work.
I can say without hesitation that the provinces which have sizeable official language minorities have made a lot of efforts and progress in that area since last year, and that the provincial ministers of justice concerned gave me full co-operation on this. I think that the will of parliament in that regard was very clearly expressed last year and that the attorneys general and the provincial ministers of justice gave us continuous co-operation in order to offer to their citizens the services which are provided for in that piece of legislation.
