The House resumed from Thursday, March 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-29, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and to make other related amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to continue the debate on Bill C-29, from where we left off yesterday, at which time I was addressing certain remarks on the value, merit, or demerit if you like, of mortgage interest deductibility schemes and schemes to provide deduction for real estate taxes in terms of stimulating the housing industry in this country.

I had pointed out that a number of us, a bipartisan parliamentary group, had conducted a fairly in-depth analysis of the experience of our neighbours in the United States in this particular area. I should like very briefly to reiterate that no positive decision to introduce mortgage interest deductibility or real estate tax deductibility as a policy matter has ever been adopted in the United States. It is part, if you like, of the basic structure of the U.S. revenue system, having existed since 1913 and extending not only to real estate taxes but to other local taxes, and extending not only to mortgage interest but to all interest. Therefore, I think it is important for us to recognize, when comparing our situation in Canada to that of our U.S. neighbours, that no option has ever existed in recent years for the United States to introduce such a scheme. The only option has been, of course, to withdraw such a scheme.
We were advised by all observers in the United States that the elimination of this particular provision of the law would be impossible, for a number of reasons which are quite obvious. First of all, many people who have purchased homes are, of course, dependent upon mortgage financing and upon the deductibility of interest associated with those mortgages. Basically they are in the position where the withdrawal of that benefit at this point could have severe personal economic consequences, not to speak, of course, of the very serious political difficulties of withdrawing a plan which is supported by a large number of home owners in the United States.
It was our experience, and I believe this was mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) in the course of a number of her comments both inside and outside the House, that privately many individuals whom she had encountered supported mortgage interest deductibility because they personally found it beneficial. I can assure the House that the same would be true in this country. I can think of nothing more attractive for many Canadian home owners, myself included, than to have the benefit of being able to deduct the interest which we pay on our mortgages and the real estate taxes we pay to our municipalities. That would be the personal preference, I am sure, of a wide cross-section of Canadians, and maybe of many members of this House.
When it comes to an issue of this importance, I suggest that the public interest must be placed ahead of our own personal interests here as individuals and as parliamentarians. We must look at this kind of plan in terms of what it can provide to Canadians in meeting certain fiscal, social and economic objectives.
What are those objectives? I analyse the objectives of any scheme of this kind as falling essentially into three categories. One, of course, is the social objective which has been put forward, namely, that of stimulating home ownership. As I indicated in the course of my remarks last night, we could probably find unanimity on that objective as being a desirable one for Canadians. It would also be a social objective to assist people to improve their housing accommodation and perhaps obtain some relief from the care and costs of housing accom-
March 2, 1979

modation. Those 1 would put in the area of social objectives which I believe are really germane to this debate on Bill C-29.
The fiscal objectives of any plan should be to provide a more efficient, effective and, above all, equitable tax structure. When I think of equity in terms of the tax structure-and 1 am sure that members of the opposition will agree with me-1 think of creating as much neutrality in the tax system as possible. That is, people in the same financial circumstances should bear the same amount of tax.
Finally, there is an over-all economic objective which has been put forward in support of this kind of scheme, namely that it would provide some stimulus to the economy by increasing home construction, home purchasing and concomitant consumer spending on furnishings, home improvements and so on. Those seem to be the principal objectives of any scheme of this kind.
Surely, we must look at this question of mortgage interest deductibility and real estate tax deductibility in terms of how well it achieves those objectives, on the assumption that we accept those objectives, as opposed to other techniques designed to achieve the same purposes.
One of the most significant objectives, in my opinion, of Bill C-29 is the providing of more and better housing accommodation and more ownership for Canadians. It is apparent that mortgage interest deductibility and real estate deductibility favour home owners. I am not arguing at this stage whether that is good or bad; I am simply saying that that is the result of this kind of program. By its very nature it provides more discretionary disposable income to those Canadians who find themselves in the higher income tax brackets. When we look at home ownership we find that more homes are owned by people in higher income tax brackets than people in lower income tax brackets. Obviously, it does much less to encourage the acquisition of homes by those persons who find themselves at the lower end of the income scale-
Tell that to the tenants.

-such as young couples and others who are seeking to obtain housing. My hon. friend the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) has referred to tenants, and the bill does nothing whatever for that category. Essentially, the deductions that are suggested would tend to widen the gap in terms of housing accommodation between the upper income groups and the lower income groups. My value judgment on that situation is that it is bad.
It may be-and I will return to this later-that many home owners in this country feel that they are prejudiced by high rates of taxation and that they should be provided with some form of relief. They may very well be prejudiced by high rates of taxation, and it is unquestionably true that this measure would provide those people with some form of relief. The question is, however, should that be an objective of a mortgage interest deductibility program as opposed to seeking to provide additional housing to a particular group who require housing in this country?
Housing
As has been mentioned by other members who have addressed this subject, any plan of this kind has far-reaching implications which can only be measured after rather sophisticated econometric and other studies have been conducted. For example, it was mentioned by one speaker that this kind of program of mortgage interest deductibility and real estate tax deductibility, appealing as it does to middle and upper income groups, might tend to attract those people into some of the city cores who would renovate the housing in that area-as I understand has been the case in certain areas of the United States-to the detriment of the core's existing tenant population, which is largely composed of people from lower income groups. Surely that cannot be regarded as a desirable social consequence of this kind of program.
Moving from the social objectives to the fiscal objectives, which I defined as seeking to provide more equity and more tax neutrality, it is obvious that this kind of program does not favour tax neutrality because it creates a benefit to home owners but not to existing tenants. It does not create the same benefits to people who find themselves in essentially the same financial circumstances. Therefore, it offends the principle of tax neutrality.
As I mentioned last night, there would obviously be, as we were advised by observers in the United States, a shift of local taxation into the real estate tax sector because, clearly, if a real property owner can obtain a tax deduction in that particular area but not in terms of other local taxes, then the municipalities or other local governments would be encouraged to increase the taxes in that particular area. Also, the economic objectives cannot be met through this particular plan as well as they could be met through other kinds of plans. Specifically, because the creation of additional disposable discretionary income finds its way to the higher income groups, there is less likelihood that it will find its way back to the economic stream as quickly as it would if it favoured lower income groups and people at the lower end of the scale, who basically are more consumer oriented, as statistics have shown us.
Perhaps more significant-and 1 would like all members of the House to focus on this-is the fact that, as our U.S. neighbours have told us, once this scheme is incorporated into our system, for the reasons I have already outlined it is impossible to remove it. Therefore, as I have indicated, it cannot be regarded as an economic tool. An economic tool is something which can be applied in a counter-cyclical fashion to stimulate the economy when stimulus is required and to cool off the economy when it should be cooled off. Yet here we run the risk of incorporating something structurally into our system which will be there for all time once it is introduced. Therefore, as an economic tool it is simply not viable.
I have a certain kinship with the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) who preceded me in the debate on this bill. I believe, though I stand to be corrected, that at one time he was opposed to the concept of mortgage interest deductibility, but last night he effectively supported the concept. My kinship with him is that I am almost a mirror image of the hon. member for Rosedale, in that at one time I suggested that

March 2, 1979
Housing
mortgage interest deductibility be introduced as an alternative to the registered home ownership savings plan. Subsequently, upon further examination and taking into account only some of the issues which I have raised during the course of these comments, I determined that it would not accomplish these objectives. I then moved toward a tax credit plan and have effectively supported that idea since that time, provided it is economically feasible for the country to introduce any kind of scheme at this point. I say this with a certain amount of humility, recognizing that I have had a change of position based upon a further appreciation of the very serious consequences of the introduction of this kind of scheme. I say this not in any way to denigrate the position of the progressive conservative party who brought the spotlight to bear on this issue-for that they deserve credit-but I think it behooves them to re-examine this policy in light of the evidence we have and the studies which are now available, in order to determine whether it would be in the best interests of Canadians as a whole. Upon examination of the issue I am convinced that it is not. I would encourage them to review some of the material that we have prepared.
I regard this as a very serious problem which should be considered in a non-partisan way. I am prepared to make available to the opposition the analysis we have made so that there can be a better dialogue on the subject. If there are any benefits to be derived from the mortgage interest deductibility and real estate tax deductions, I should like to know what they are. If there are any, they should be considered. On the basis of the analysis that we have made, Mr. Speaker, there does not seem to be any merit to the scheme at all over other schemes, and in some ways there could be very negative aspects.
I have prepared a document for the national caucus which I would be quite happy to make available to my friends on the other side of the House. It summarizes the conclusions I arrived at on the basis of the discussions held at Washington at which the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra-who, I understand, will speak on this bill-the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae) were present.
There is no doubt that when this policy was put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) during the summer of 1978, it struck a responsive chord in certain sections of the community. I noticed it in my riding and I am sure other hon. members noticed it in theirs. I ask myself, if all these negative aspects are inherent in the plan, why did it strike such a responsive chord? Initially, I think it gives the appearance of stimulating the housing industry and encouraging home ownership. I was the victim of that illusion myself until I studied the matter in more detail. It is apparent now that it does not stimulate new housing nearly to the extent to which it stimulates, encourages, and benefits existing home owners. There are any number of other plans which would be more effective in creating new housing and bringing more people on to the housing market. If there is an objective inherent in this scheme, to provide tax relief to home owners, then there is no

doubt that objective is accomplished by the suggestion that mortgage interest and real estate taxes should be deductible.
If we wish to provide tax relief to middle and upper income people, who suffer a severe tax burden under our present tax system, I believe, should we single out home owners? Why should we not consider our fiscal system as a whole and try to make it more fair and create more tax neutrality in all areas to which it applies? That is the objective I have been working toward for several years. It is one of the reasons why I sought to become a member of parliament, so that I could become involved in the area of fiscal reform which I believe to be so important.
It bothers me to think that we would consider introducing a provision of this kind which would further exacerbate the problems which I, and others involved in fiscal matters, have been attempting to eliminate. For example, home owners feel disadvantaged because their real estate taxes and mortgage interest payments are not deductible. If we take two Canadians, each of whom has an amount of available capital with which to buy the average priced house in Canada-which I understand is in the neighbourhood of $60,000-the question is whether the one who buys the home is better off than the one who receives interest income from his $60,000 which, assuming a 50 per cent bracket, at 10 per cent, nets $3,000 after tax. He then has that amount available for rental accommodation. I suggest that there are not too many Canadians who would prefer the position of the man with $3,000 after tax income available for living accommodation to that of the man who owns the $60,000 home, even with the costs which he has to support.
It may sound sophisticated, Mr. Speaker, but all economists have established that there is a real benefit to living in your own home. There is an imputed rental value to be attached to that benefit which, until 1963, was actually subject to taxation in the United Kingdom. We should not be horrified to learn that it has even been considered by other countries in the western world. There is a real benefit to be attached to home ownership by the mere fact of living in the house, which has never been taxed. I am hopeful and confident that it will never be taxed. Nevertheless, the home owner is in a much better situation than the renter in the same financial circumstances.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we have the advantage in Canada that a capital gain on the principal residence is not taxable, irrespective of whether the vendor intends to buy another home. The United States has recently adopted a provision which exempts a once in a lifetime $100,000 gain. First of all, however, the home owner must be aged 55 or over and must have owned the house for at least seven years and lived in it for a certain period during those seven years. Our provisions are infinitely more attractive than those of the United States in this regard.
If we want to attain these objectives, Mr. Speaker, and provide that more people can own homes, we must look at programs which will be effective in bringing about that situation. The tax credit scheme is one because it treats people at the high end of the scale and people at the low end of the scale
March 2, 1979

equally. If we were to establish a refundable tax credit, that would reach the lower economic levels of our society and provide them with money to enable them to have adequate housing.
It is important to recognize that these schemes are costly, Mr. Speaker. Fiscal responsibility requires that no scheme of this magnitude be introduced without the most thorough analysis of the economic consequences, both in terms of stimulation of the economy and in terms of increased government deficit.
There are better ways of providing home ownership, Mr. Speaker, and there are many better ways of bringing equity into the fiscal system. This scheme would basically create a further departure from the principle of tax neutrality which I find to be unacceptable. Accordingly, I think all members of the House should address themselves, over the next several years, to the question of how our fiscal system can be improved. There is no question that there are inequities in it. This program, however, would not improve the fiscal system but would merely worsen it.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as an instrument of economic stimulus this scheme would not be effective. It would favour people at the upper end of the bracket who, by and large, are not the consuming public, and it could never be eliminated from our system.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize that this is not something I approach in a partisan way. At one point, as I said, I supported the idea. I think that together in this country we should seek the best possible means of providing home ownership to more Canadians. I beseech the Conservative opposition not to suggest that a mortgage interest deductibility plan and a real estate tax deductibility plan be foisted on the Canadian public, with all the serious long-term economic consequences it could have.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-29, the housing legislation we have been discussing in our spare time, when there is nothing else to do, because this is the way we have been doing it since the minister put the bill forward a number of days ago. This strengthens my opinion that the bill has been badly put together, it is incomplete and very difficult to understand. I have been wondering, if we passed the bill as it is, whether the regulations to be enacted would be so different we would not recognize the act anymore.
My feeling is we will have to be very careful in committee with this legislation, and the minister will have to be well prepared to give us the information needed, mainly on the criteria referred to in certain clauses of the bill. There is mention of standards and criteria in a number of places, but no explanation is given and we have no sure indication where those criteria might lead us. We have no clear idea who will
Housing
establish those criteria or construction standards, the standards for establishing lending values. The experience with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is that they have numerous offices across Canada and it would seem there were just as many National Housing Acts as there are CMHC offices. If we are to compare for instance the way the act is implemented in the area served by the Val d'Or office with that of another office in the lower St. Lawrence or the Montreal area, we would think the act is different because there is so much difference.
I suggest there should be uniformity, even if flexibility must be maintained to meet the needs and weather conditions in various areas. Building in southern Ontario is quite different from building in northern Quebec. But when it comes to lending values and valuation, I feel that variations are too wide and it is hard to assess the basis used to determine valuation rates and lending values. Mr. Speaker, in his introduction the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has praised the National Housing Act. Obviously he dealt only with the bright side of the story. He surely was not going to, nor did 1 expect him to, openly criticize all the shortcomings in the act. Yet in his speech he told us over and over again that most Canadians enjoy good housing.
I have tried to grasp what the minister meant by that when he said that most Canadians have good housing. Did he mean that Canadians live in luxurious houses, that they live in very comfortable houses, houses in which they want to live or rather did the minister mean to say that Canadians live in expensive houses? This brings us to the issue of programs developed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, these loan programs which we have had for several years, one formerly called AHOP and now rebaptized GMP, and all these types of loans which have been promoted. Most of these loans were designed for moderate income people. When one studies what is happening in the case of these people, one will realize that they actually live in very expensive houses. It does not mean that they live in luxurious houses, far from it.
1 have before me a brochure published by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which explains the new GMP program-the graduated mortgage payments program. We are given as an example a $35,000 loan at 103/4 per cent over 25 years. Under the old program which called for equal payments over 25 years, the reimbursement of such a mortgage would cost $99,300. Under the new graduated mortgage payments program this $35,000 mortgage at 103/4 per cent will in the end cost $108,864. I therefore conclude, Mr. Speaker, that most Canadians who have availed themselves of our housing legislation live in houses which are much too expensive in relation to the size of their income. When these houses are sold, it is natural that developers and builders do not mention it because they are under no obligation to do so but in the end when the buyer is through paying for his house, it will have cost him over $100,000 to get a house which is very little more than

March 2, 1979
Housing
four walls, a roof and foundations. The house is far from luxurious, it is just good enough to live decently in, nothing more.
Developers and builders tell buyers: Thanks to payment facilities, thanks to easy loans, all you will have to pay is so much every month during so many years. A young couple who want to live in their home and who want to own a house do not realize the full extent of the commitment they are about to sign; they see only what they are going to pay, only the difference between what they will have to pay to own a house and what they are paying now as tenants. People are being lured with that difference but the truth and the reality are quite different. I do think that if every prospective owner sat down to count how much money he will have spent to buy his house over 25 or 30 years, many of them would think twice before buying and would not dare commit themselves that way. They might come up with another solution. That is exactly what is happening now, and many young couples prefer to deal with builders and developers rather than build their houses themselves and get a mortgage loan elsewhere in order to avoid lengthy and costly commitments they would have to make if they were to deal with CMHC.
This means, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that this housing program does not really meet the needs of Canadian people, the needs of the people this legislation is designed to help, because there are three main groups of people in Canada, those with a large income or with enough savings to do without lenders, banks, trust companies, insurance companies if they build a house. They are well off and have enough money to pay for their house when they buy it or have it built. The next group, perhaps the largest, is made up of people with low incomes who do not have enough savings to pay cash for their houses. Therefore, they have to borrow money, to deal with authorized lenders, with banks or credit unions, trust companies or insurance companies to obtain housing loans. Those are perhaps the most hard up.
The third group, Mr. Speaker, is probably made up of people who do not want or need to own a home because they are mobile, as it were. They live in a town or village for a few months, to work on a job and then they move on to another village. They are always on the move because of their jobs, or still they may be handicapped or disabled and do not think of or feel like buying a house.
Mr. Speaker, our housing legislation was designed to meet the needs of people in the largest group in making easier terms and easier loan facilities available to them so they can become home owners. But they were really tricked because by holding out to them these easier loans, they were forced to pay unduly high interest rates compared to their incomes.
At the present time, in my area at least, interest rates are about 10%, 11 and 11% per cent. Mr. Speaker, when one

agrees to repay a $35,000 mortgage over a 25- or 30-year period, we have to think twice about it because it is a commitment to pay very high interests over a very long period. The new program the minister is promoting so much may seem attractive to young couples who want to become homeowners because at first, for about ten years, the payments will be a little less since they are not paying any interest at that time. Interests will accrue and will be charged only from the seventh year. I think that once again, Mr. Speaker, they foisted the program upon the public rather like pressure salesmen. The government is quite good at submitting attractive programs, but in the end people who want to borrow to buy a house will have to pay about $10,000 more.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would have been much better to lower the interest rates to help young couples buy a house. A few years ago, through a special program, interest rates were lowered to 8 per cent in certain cases while the current rates were about 9'/2 per cent or 10 per cent. This nearly was the same as subsidizing new homeowners.
1 believe that if we want to be logical and help everyone make his dream of owning his own house come true in Canada, we must find the means to lower considerably the interest rates on mortgage loans. Otherwise, we shall never achieve this objective. We shall always be tenants in our own homes. We shall always have payments to make, because I can assure you that not many people will see the end of 25 year mortgages as there are not many houses built today which can last 25 or 30 years without costly repairs and maintenance jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to underline this once again and ask the minister and the government to find the means to lower mortgage interest rates so that they do not exceed 6 per cent. This would be much more effective than any other suggestion made either by the Progressive Conservative party, the New Democratic Party or even the Liberal party. We can criticize any suggestion that is made, but if we do not take the means to enable low income people to find housing without putting too much pressure on their income and forcing them to seek out loan companies, I believe that we shall have failed in our duty and that we shall never succeed as well as we should in providing appropriate housing for everyone.
Mr. Speaker, we have all we need to build homes. We hardly have to import anything from other countries, as we produce our own building materials, such as structural materials and lumber, and we have a great many sawmills producing high quality lumber, we have plants that produce all kinds of materials used in the construction and production of these houses. I cannot understand why the cost of homes remains so high. Obviously the cost of housing has gone up because of wages and all sorts of overhead that go into the cost of producing houses.
I have here a chart from the Quebec Provincial Home Builders Association which mentions nine different trades connected with home building. For each one of them, which
March 2, 1979

include carpenters, bricklayers, cement finishers, roofers, and so on, the builder must pay, over and above wages, which in Quebec, for a carpenter for example, is $10.28 an hour, nine other items such as holidays, social security, the Office de la construction du Quebec, unemployment insurance, Workmen's Compensation Board, Quebec Pension Plan, medicare, wage compensation fund and so forth, nine items, for a total of $2.76 which is added to the worker's salary.
There are also the administrative costs which the builder must assume and which are passed on to the customer. There is also a fair profit of 10 per cent, so that if a carpenter is paid $10.28 an hour, the customer is billed $17.93 an hour for his services. Therefore, it is not the carpenter alone who is expensive, but all those who are involved in a construction project. There are about ten other people who must get paid in addition to the carpenter. All these elements certainly contribute to the high cost of housing.
On top of that, Mr. Speaker, we have interest rates which are over 10 per cent. In fact, they are about 11% per cent just now. I suggest therefore that it is almost impossible and unthinkable for young Canadians to become the owners of their own houses, without restricting themselves on such items as food, lodging, medical care, education and so on. I suggest this bill needs improvements if we want the National Housing Act to meet the needs of Canadians and of those who require assistance to become home owners.
During committee meetings, I hope that all those who have a brief to submit, advice to give and recommendations to make to the minister will be heard, in order to improve this bill, so that the Housing Act may better meet the needs and fulfil the expectation of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to take part in this debate unexpectedly, and with a mixture of sadness and anger. I say that my participation today at second reading of Bill C-29 is unexpected, in the sense that the problem in my riding 1 am about to describe came to my attention as a surprising first assignment as a member of parliament immediately following my election in Hamilton-Wentworth last October 16. The sadness I feel this afternoon stems from a personal investigation of a CMHC horror story and a first-hand feeling of the helplessness and frustration experienced by many of my constituents. My anger mounts when I realize that the situation I am about to describe is not confined to one condominium development sliding into a ravine but to several other badly executed housing projects in Hamilton and, indeed, across the country.
The countless other horror stories which are coming to light in this debate may not be as spectacular as 100 Quigley Road in east end Hamilton, but the principal failure of the federal government's role in this near tragedy for my constituents is typical of the chaos which has enveloped CMHC because of
Housing
inadequate inspections and the use of substandard building materials.
Like other hon. members on this side of the House, I want to go on record as saying that the bill before the House contains many good features, some of which are long overdue, but I also wish to register the concern of my colleagues on this side of the House that these National Housing Act amendments deserve, indeed, demand, close scrutiny in the standing committee, although I am beginning to wonder whether we members of the opposition will have much opportunity to carry out the kind of detailed examination needed. This has something to do with an election, and that is why I am taking this opportunity this afternoon to raise a particular concern of mine relating to this bill, namely, the program which will replace the Assisted Home Ownership Program. I want to get my experience and the very real worries of my constituents on the record now so that the government will be in no doubt as to the official opposition's criticism and suggested remedies once we hit the campaign trail.
AHOP was, and is, a good idea. It is the government's execution of that idea which has created so many problems across the country. AHOP has succeeded in making affordable housing available to people who normally would not be able to afford to buy homes, even if the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) calls owning one's own home a luxury. That is not our view, and notwithstanding the comments made by the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston), there are countless hundreds of thousands of Canadians in the middle and lower income brackets who are tenants and whose dream it is to own their own homes some day. My leader's mortgage interest deductibility proposal, as has been pointed out in this debate, is aimed at that vast and important constituency. People are responding to that constructive proposal, which offers them hope of achieving their dream.
And so did AHOP offer hope, but in the government's haste to cash in on the building boom of the mid-1970s and the desire of people to own condominiums, that hope has long since turned into financial and personal nightmares for too many Canadians who took this government and its program at their word. As some of my colleagues have pointed out, it is the same thing all over again: inadequate inspections, disgraceful construction and design, and the use of substandard building materials.
I will deal in a moment with the charge of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) that we on this side of the House are raising only isolated incidents.
Let me tell the House how I first came to learn of what I thought was just an isolated incident at 100 Quigley Road in Hamilton. The very first weekend following the October 16 by-election 1 received an urgent message through my Stoney Creek constituency office from Mr. and Mrs. Keith Parks. When I called back, they informed me that several units in their condominium development were slowly sliding into a 50 to 75-foot deep ravine. Apparently the units had been built too close to the edge of the ravine, and the developer had not packed down properly some 13 to 17 feet of fill. Furthermore,

March 2, 1979
Housing
he used inferior chemically-treated fill. This resulted in soil erosion, then cracks and, finally, a fear on the part of several tenants that one more winter of weighty snow or an accompanying heavy spring run-off, and whole back yards, patios and family rooms could end up at the bottom of the Red Hill Ravine.
The physical threat to the tenants of 100 Quigley Road, not to mention all the little kiddies who were playing around the edge of that erosion, was frightening enough, but Mr. and Mrs. Parks had another incredible piece of news for me.
The condominium tenants were under a city of Hamilton court order to effect immediate repairs to the erosion. Construction was to begin not later than November 22, 1978, and it would cost $30,000. Failure to meet the deadline and complete these repairs would result in a $10,000 fine being levied against the condominium owners. In any event, I was told that the people at 100 Quigley Road were to be assessed an extra $200 per unit on their mortgages. Being hit with that news during the Christmas shopping season, needless to say, had these folks mighty upset.
The question to their new member of parliament was what could 1 do to convince Ottawa that none of this was the fault of the condominium owners, and was there a possibility of a $30,000 federal grant or loan until the repairs were carried out? The owners eventually settled on a loan. They were determined to pay it all back. My first reaction on hearing this story, frankly, was that of a television newsman: "What a visual story this will be!" Did anybody else know about 100 Quigley Road? No, said Mr. and Mrs. Parks, people were afraid to let the media know about their plight because the resulting publicity could damage the credibility of their housing project, but would I please come and talk with the unit owners and see the situation for myself?
I agreed to treat this first case as a member of parliament on the confidential basis that the public comes to expect from its elected representatives. However, there is one element in my journalistic background which I could not set aside. In a case like this I felt it vitally important to conduct a personal investigation into both sides of the story. This I have done in connection with this case. One hundred Quigley Road started as a rental townhouse project in 1974. Like so many other housing starts, this was during the boom of the mid-seventies, those halcyon days which the Canadian construction industry remembers now with misty eyes. At any rate, in 1975, 100 Quigley Road quickly changed to a condominium project called the Wentworth Condominium Corporation No. 20, registered in September, 1975, and including 150 units.
The financing was originally a blanket mortgage through CMHC. It was replaced with individual CMHC mortgages, and by the end of 1975 all the units were occupied. That is a point to which I will come back a little later.
It was during the spring of 1976 that a soil erosion problem became evident. The land fill behind several of the units on the north slope of the ravine began disappearing, and finally things

began happening in the units themselves as they settled. By September of 1978 a crack had appeared in the ground within seven feet of units 62, 63 and 64, and the land started to slide. Cracks also appeared in the basement of the affected units. Second floor toilets leaked through the vestibule ceilings, and family rooms began to sag.
Consulting engineers were immediately retained to analyse the problem, and in the meantime Hamilton's building department issued a court order to make the north slope between units 54 to 62 more stable. I should point out that the units in question were built on the north and west slopes of that ravine. The north slope is the most precarious; the west slope could withstand this and perhaps next winter's snow, but inevitably several other units face a similar caving in. The consulting engineers' report made recommendations for shoring up the units, at a cost of $30,000 for the 150 unit owners. The north slope needing immediate repairs would cost $18,000, the west slope would require $12,000 worth of restoration.
That news hit the 100 Quigley Road condominium tenants on October 16, 1978. By this time, my newsman's sense, 1 must admit, was getting the better of me. I have kept 100 Quigley Road a private matter, but by now, several members of the Wentworth condominium board of directors and I felt that no useful purpose would be served by keeping this scandal quiet any longer. I decided to raise the matter in the House of Commons and let the media take it from there to the public. Frankly, what spurred me on was the Virginia Drive project raised by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). In December, during the question period, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs had roundly castigated my colleague for raising the matter, saying it was just an "isolated incident". The minister knew then, and he knows now very well, that Virgina Drive was anything but an isolated incident involving CMHC funded housing projects.
If Virginia Drive was an isolated incident, then why did one of his senior CMHC officials tell me that even if the corporation could lend the Quigley Road people the $30,000 to shore up the ravine, he refused on the grounds that:
It would open up the flood gates to similar requests across Canada.
The Minister of State for Urban Affairs, in his answer to my question one day in the House of Commons, said "yes", that was why he turned down a grant or loan to the people of 100 Quigley Road.
Hon. members on the government side will probably think that we in the opposition-and I, specifically in these remarks-have been embarking on a CMHC bashing exercise by raising the kind of situation I been have discussing. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker.
What really made me realize that we are on the right track to detail cases such as 100 Quigley Road in Hamilton and the Virginia Drive problem in St. John's, Newfoundland, and pursue the government for its sheer negligence in these situations, was a chance meeting I had during a brief vacation in January. By staggering coincidence, a young couple staying at our hotel in the Caribbean used to live in the city of Hamilton.
March 2, 1979

It was several days before I discovered that the fellow with whom I had had several casual conversations was an inspector with CMHC and in fact had worked on projects in and around the Red Hill Creek area of Hamilton, including 100 Quigley Road. He could not be certain that the units which were sliding into the ravine had been his exact responsibility, but he knew the CMHC personnel on site at the time. What he told me, on a not for attribution basis, confirmed my worst suspicions about why these, and who knows how many hundreds of other AHOP customers, have been going through incredible inconvenience in recent years. I should point out that the CMHC inspector in question now works in another part of Canada, but his memory is vivid on the corporation's role regarding 100 Quigley Road.
This inspector told me that an initial on site inspection of the location, the plans, and the construction of a CMHC approved projects, was always supposed to be followed up by supplementary visits. However, during this particular period in the mid-1970s, when there was a real construction boom and many hundreds of condominium projects were being thrown up, CMHC simply did not have the manpower available to carry out their supplementary inspections. My informant says that he cannot understand how he or his fellow inspectors could have missed the danger signals which were so apparent with the construction of these units at Quigley Road so close to the edge of the ravine. He is certain that a supplementary visit by a CMHC inspector, indeed two or three supplementary visits, would have discovered the slipshod methods being used in the land-fill procedure to shore up the rear of the units. But, he said, "obviously, somebody wasn't watching what was going on."
That, to me, is a pretty damning indictment of the lack of responsibility assumed by the federal government housing agency. My informant went on to explain that there were several other projects in the east Hamilton area going on at the same time and that I would probably discover similar, if not as spectacular, cases as 100 Quigley Road. He was reading my mind, because shortly thereafter I brought the Red Hill ravine problem to the attention of the Hamilton media when I, along with other Hamilton area political representatives, began receiving complaints and horror stories from nearby condominium projects, all of them initially financed and inspected under AHOP.
Let me introduce to you very briefly the case of Mr. Godwin Charles who lives in unit 26 No. 11 Glen Vista Drive, about half a mile away from 100 Quigley Road. Mr. Charles outlined a weird problem he was having in his kitchen and invited me to drop around and experience for myself what had become for Mr. Charles and his family an intolerable situation. It was on a clear, cold Saturday afternoon in late November that I visited unit 26, a fashionable, comfortable, indeed cosy looking split-level condominium unit on Glen Vista Drive. It was cosy looking, but anything but cosy feeling.
As you enter the front door and go down a small hallway, you come upon a very compact and comfortable looking living room. There is a half flight of stairs to another hallway on the
Housing
mezzanine level which has a dining room and leads to several bedrooms. But at the top of the stairway is the kitchen, which is built over the garage, and looks out on to Glen Vista Drive. The kitchen is positively frigid, a good 20 degrees cooler than the rest of the house. I can hear hon. members interjecting and asking, "How cold was it?" It was so cold that liquids under the kitchen sink froze if left there for just a few hours, so cold that you could feel the wind blowing through electric light sockets. The Charles' cannot heat anything on their stove, even with the burners turned up full because of the blast of cold air that is coming down through the vent above the stove.
That's really cool.

Ah, you say, that is because the kitchen is built over the garage, and any kitchens built directly over enclosed garages are likely to experience this drop in temperature, or the windows are not fitted properly and the cold is seeping into the kitchen that way, or maybe there is faulty insulation under the kitchen floor or in the walls facing the street. I was astounded to learn two things; neither of the obvious faults that come to mind was apparent in the case of Godwin Charles' kitchen; and that his unit was one of many up and down Glen Vista Drive experiencing the same insufferable inconvenience. Not only was it an insufferable inconvenience, but an expensive one. The cold air which fills the kitchen sweeps down the small staircase and makes the sitting room below quite uncomfortable. Only the bedrooms are liveable, but in the meantime the heating bills of the Charles' family and their neighbours on Glen Vista Drive have skyrocketed since this problem was first discovered more than a year ago.
Hon. members might be interested to know that 1 personally checked out each of the possible design faults which would result in the freezing kitchens. The covered garages immediately below the kitchens are warmer than the kitchens. There is plenty of insulation in the walls of the garage and in the ceiling immediately below the kitchens. Some of the unit owners have even taped clear vinyl coverings inside and outside the windows to cut down on the cold but without luck. Explanations have been offered that a kitchen located below a garage with a sloping roof inevitably causes temperature problems.
In any event, now it is up to the individual condominium unit owners, on top of the $42,000 price tag on each unit, to invest what they can or must to rectify this most unusual problem, which clearly is either a design fault by the builder, inferior insulation material, or both. As in the case of 100 Quigley Road, it is the buyer who gets caught between faulty design, materials and inspection on the one hand, and a passing of the buck between one level of government to another, and to another, when it comes to redressing these totally unexpected and highly unjustified inconveniences experienced by these home owners.

March 2, 1979
Housing
The entire AHOP program from the outset should have been labelled like cigarette packages which warn of danger to smokers' health. Every AHOP project should have been labelled, "Buyer beware." Had many of my constituents known the inconvenience and heartache they were about to experience when they took advantage of the federal government's generous offer to assist in their home buying, they would not be living in 100 Quigley Road or in No. 11 Glen Vista Drive today. Indeed, many of them no longer live there.
At Quigley Road 32 owners have defaulted on their mortgages. It is small wonder. The units at 100 Quigley Road were all purchased in 1975 on the AHOP program. A reduced mortgage was paid for the first five years. Mrs. Parks complains that she is paying $233 a month for her three-bedroom unit, and without AHOP she would have been paying $353 a month. That is fine, however, but by 1980 she will have to start paying the higher rate and will owe 120 per cent of the original value of the unit, or about $9,000 more. One must add to that prospect the escalating levy to each unit owner to effect repairs or maintenance because of poor quality workmanship inside the units and on the landscaping.
The value of the units at 100 Quigley Road will not exactly be bargain basement prices for house hunters. By 1980, when the payments suddenly increase and owners start to find that they owe 120 per cent on their homes, a tidal wave of defaults may start to occur. It is an awful prospect, and by 1981 perhaps 100 Quigley Road will be a ghost town. I wonder how many similar potential ghost towns, or how many hundreds of other 100 Quigley Roads there are across Canada. That is why I was so angry when the Minister of State for Urban Affairs had the unmitigated audacity to suggest the situations raised by the hon. member for St. John's East and the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) are isolated incidents and are not indicative of the government's excellent federal housing policy. One just has to ask the people of Quigley Road or Glen Vista Drive how isolated they feel right now.
Like the constituents I represent, I guess my real sense of frustration lies in the lack of responsiblity which the federal government feels it should take in situations like 100 Quigley Road. As a reporter I became sick and tired of buck passing between one level of government to the other. As a member of parliament, not just reporting on the plight of people caught in the bureaucratic web but representing them, I am even more exasperated at the failure of the federal government to live up to its responsibility. My people in Hamilton, and untold thousands of other people in hundreds of projects across the country, believed in the government's promise to make it easier for them to acquire their own homes. They were not told they would have to contend with city bylaws, provincial conservation authority regulations and, above all, improper inspection and negligence on the part of the federal government's housing authority.
I, and the minister, know that the entire blame for situations like 100 Quigley Road does not lie at the feet of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In this case the local contractor, Lucille Investments Limited, and the city of

Hamilton building inspectors, share some responbility for the problem. According to city bylaws, two or three of those units should not have been built at all. Authorization was made on the basis of drawings and not by on-site inspection. In 1975 when the builder applied to make the units at Quigley Road into a condominium project, the provincial conservation authority reported that the project should be rejected because the homes had to be built not closer than 25 feet to the edge of the ravine.
The case I am making against CMHC basically is one of moral neglect of the owners, who originally were enticed by the corporation into buying these homes. As I have pointed out, the method of inspection by CMHC is spotty at best, and to repeat the words of my CMHC inspector friend, "Somebody was not watching what was going on."
Typical of the government's attitude is the following quote from a letter which the Minister of State for Urban Affairs recently sent to Mrs. June Collins, the director of the Quigley Road Condominium Corporation:
Unfortunately, there is no authority under the National Housing Act which would permit Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make a grant to your corporation to cover the cost of the necessary remedial work. 1 regret that CMHC is unable to be of assistance in resolving the soil erosion problem.
The minister described the Quigley Road problems as being "unforeseen expenditures". Members of the House cannot imagine how much at a loss these condominium owners feel when they receive this kind of reply from a minister of the government. Perhaps if anyone is listening on the government side they will understand how infuriated I am that good and decent people, like those I have met at 100 Quigley Road, should find themselves in a physical and financial bind over which they had no control, in the first place, and for which they should not have responsibility now.
Surely the bottom line to this litany of personal tragedies and disasters recorded during this debate is some responsibility on the part of the government. Surely the minister has some compassion for what we on this side have shown are not isolated incidents but regular occurrences in the government's national housing agency. The minister must realize CMHC is in a mess, and that a full public accounting is needed before even more millions of taxpayers' dollars are wasted on this corporation. It is nothing short of a political tool of the government. I conclude by referring to the lead editorial in the February 3 edition of the Hamilton Spectator. "It's time to evaluate CMHC".
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I will add another chapter to this debate, one of sorrow and bungling. It demonstrates what the government has accomplished in the last ten years since it professed to be the champion of the just society in 1968.
I do not wish to take away from the thrust of the argument I will make, the argument of the poor people who comprise 20 per cent of our population. These people hoped the government would fulfil its promise respecting housing. I do not want to

take away from the thrust of this argument, so may I call it four o'clock?
