He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to my private member's bill, Bill C-219, I share with the House that the intent of this piece of legislation is to reinstate capital punishment for crimes of high treason or premeditated murder.
On July 14, 1976, this House abolished capital punishment under legislation known as Bill C-84. It is interesting when we review the vote on third reading to find that there were just six votes difference, an extremely thin margin. I spoke on third reading at that time and stated it was a sad day for participatory democracy because surveys indicated at that time, as they still indicate today, that 75 per cent to 80 per cent of the Canadian people wished to retain capital punishment for premeditated and planned murder. To this date I still fail to understand what makes individual members of parliament feel their conscience is so much wiser than the collective conscience of the Canadian people.
It was stated in this House by members of the government party that we were to free ourselves in Canada of that ordeal known as capital punishment, but that is not the case. The government has not given the House any indication of what its plans are regarding the introduction of amendments to the National Defence Act. I understand this act presently provides capital punishment for 36 offences, some of them as strange as an individual getting drunk while on watch. We do not have total abolition in Canada simply because this act has not been amended and there are these provisions contained in the National Defence Act. I would appreciate very much some guidance from government members as to what the government's intentions are in dealing with the National Defence Act itself. We find that we are discriminating against one segment of our society in the armed forces because of this provision for capital punishment still in the legislation.
Capital punishment is not an issue in respect of which party politics should become involved. It involves a decision that individual members in this chamber have to make within themselves, and vote accordingly. It is imperative that we truly have a free vote in this chamber, not only like the vote in 1976. It was supposedly free, but in reality it was not. We saw cabinet members en masse vote for abolition of capital punishment, but it was obvious to me when watching the voting on the other side that some disciplinary action, even though it was not overly obvious, had been taken in regard to some of the backbench members as well.
Not true.

If we are to have a truly free vote in the House of Commons it should be conducted as it was in 1966 when four private members sponsored a bill at that time, without any obligation on the cabinet or any member to support a piece of government legislation, as was the case in respect of Bill C-84 in 1976. That is the commitment the leader of this party has given to the Canadian people, that we will have a

March 2, 1979
Criminal Code
truly free vote on this issue in the House of Commons by allowing a vote on a private member's bill, or a series of private members' bills on which each and every member of this House would have a free vote. Members will have no obligation to support government legislation because it will be a private member's bill and we will have freedom to vote for the reinstatement of capital punishment or the retention of abolition.
I also found it somewhat surprising to note the attitude of members opposite in dealing with the referendum legislation. They wish to go to the people on a question as to whether they wish to see our country separated. It is obvious to me there are very few people in this nation of ours who wish to see Canada separated. They want to hear the wishes of Canadians on an issue like this, but are not interested in hearing what Canadian people have to say on an issue like capital punishment.
As I said earlier, it is a sad day for participatory democracy when members opposite close their ears to a pressing issue such as capital punishment, a very emotional issue to the majority of Canadian people. I am truly puzzled how an abolitionist can feel that his own conscience is so much wiser than the collective conscience of the Canadian people.
The incidence of violent crime in the past ten years has increased dramatically. We cannot go back just to the period of 1976 when capital punishment was abolished in this House, because in essence it was abolished in 1965 by this government. No one has been hanged in Canada since that time. Abolition may not have been approved by legislative authority before 1976, but since 1965 this government has not carried out capital punishment for any capital crime.
The evidence is inconclusive as to whether capital punishment is in reality a deterrent. Any discussion of the merits or otherwise of capital punishment goes beyond the area of politics and each person makes up his own mind according to the dictates of his conscience and his judgment.
The abolitionists claim that capital punishment is not a deterrent to would-be murderers. In my opinion this is an empty argument and completely beside the point. There is no way to determine how many murders were not committed by those who wanted to commit the act, but did not, for fear of execution. The question should be, does the supreme crime demand the supreme penalty? In effect, do we place the highest possible value on the life of the victim?
The abolitionists say capital punishment has no deterrent effect. There are no facts to prove it one way or the other, but to say that the death penalty is no deterrent is to say that men do not fear death. I find that to be a rather incredible assertion. Fear of death, in my view, is an instinctive reaction.
I would ask how many of us in this chamber do not value or fear for our lives? Life is regarded by man as a precious possession which he wishes to preserve more eagerly than anything else. He would, therefore, defend it to the utmost against every threat, including the threat of capital execution.
There must be a serious and real risk of execution for the death penalty to be an effective tool, because crime will not

decrease until being a criminal becomes more dangerous than being a victim.
The abolitionists usually state as an argument in favour of abolition that a mistake can be made in carrying out capital punishment. Although this is a valid comment, it is not a valid argument in a debate on capital punishment, because what we are discussing now is what the price should be for an individual who commits premeditated or planned murder. We are not arguing or discussing the merits of our judicial system. If there are errors in that area they must be safeguarded against; but that statement is not a valid argument in this debate because, as I said, what we have to resolve here is what to do with an individual who has been found guilty of taking another individual's life intentionally.
The very individuals we ask to give us protection deserve protection themselves, and I speak mainly of our police officers and prison guards. If what is known as capital punishment today is not reinstated, our friends who do such a superb job of law enforcement will have no protection whatsoever. What will a criminal imprisoned for life have to lose if he kills a prison guard? In reality, he will gain his freedom if his bid for escape succeeds; if he does not, he loses nothing. If capital punishment is not reinstated the prisoner in reality has nothing to lose and a great deal to gain.
I believe in capital punishment for all premeditated or planned murder, which makes up approximately 1 per cent of the murders committed in Canada. I believe it is the prime duty of the government to offer citizens protection against violent crime, and in my view capital punishment is a necessary tool to ensure that protection. That is why I have introduced Bill C-219 to amend the Criminal Code to reinstate capital punishment for premeditated and planned murder.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate being recognized and having this opportunity to add a few words to this debate. I want to say at the outset that I very much respect the right of any member of this House to express a view contrary to mine on this very controversial issue, and I respect their sincerity for that view. 1 know that the hon. member opposite who has brought forward this private member's bill has done so with the serious concern that the reinstitution of the death penalty will indeed bring better protection for the public in Canada. I cannot agree with that, and for that reason I would like to add some comments.
Back in the so-called minority parliament of 1972 to 1974, this House debated and then brought into effect a limited capital punishment bill which reduced the categories of murder that would lead to the imposition of the death penalty to the categories of killers of policemen and prison guards on duty. At that time I put forward, along with the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), outside this House a proposal, which I had hoped the government would take up, of total abolition.
I believe that in fact there are many other victims of this most terrible of all crimes other than policemen and prison
March 2, 1979

guards, who are less prepared and less aware of the risk within their lives and livelihoods of death. I speak, for instance, of assaults on children leading to death, kidnapping and death, and premeditated murder and death, although that can also be premeditated murder in the case of prison guards or policemen being killed.
At that time I brought the bill forward arguing, although I did not have the opportunity because of the system to bring it formally into the House, that what we needed was not the death penalty but more effective law, with very harsh penalties for a much broader segment of that most serious of all crimes, murder. The member for Saint-Denis and I proposed at that time substantially the same bill that the government later adopted when it abolished capital punishment in 1976. Had we acted earlier, however, we would have had for three more years what we have had since 1976.
As an abolitionist of long standing, I want to make it clear that I believe that we have a more effective law, stronger deterrence and better results for the Canadian public since the House abolished the capital punishment penalty in 1976. That law said that we would no longer have the death penalty on the books. If one measured all violent crimes on a yardstick, crimes of murder would be a very small proportion of that yardstick, and those crimes of murder which involve the killing of policemen and prison guards on duty would be a very, very small part of that measurement of murder out of the total violent crimes.
What we did was to change the law so that not only would the killers of policemen and prison guards on duty face the strictest of all possible penalties, short of society doing what it abhors most, the taking of human life. We said there would be 25 years before the consideration of parole-not released after 25 years, but 25 years before the consideration of parole, and then the possibility of parole.
In the original proposal made by the hon. member for Saint-Denis and I, we had not included the so-called "glimmer of hope" clause. The "glimmer of hope" clause which was in the law passed in 1976 says that after 15 years if one has had absolutely the highest kind of behaviour while in prison, that person will have a chance to go before a special board and have that term reduced to 15 years and then be eligible for parole. If that board of judges determines that this slim possibility can take place because of the prisoner's exemplary behaviour, the parole board can then consider parole. That parole board would have members on it from the constituency into which that convicted murderer would be released.
As an abolitionist, who first took up this cause back in the early 1960s when a journalist, and who covered the last hangings in Canada of two men called Turpin and Lucas, at the Don jail on, I believe, December 11, 1962, I think that society must have a principle beyond the emotions of any individual within that society. If we believe that we organize ourselves not only in order to care for each other and protect ourselves, but also to demonstrate to one another that we could each do better by recognizing each other, then surely a state that has reached that enlightened level should not endorse the
Criminal Code
taking of human life, which our criminal law books say is the most extreme of all crimes.
I must admit that facing the public as an elected politician both in 1972, 1973, and then again in 1976 on this issue, a public very concerned about increased rates of violent crime, I felt an obligation to offer them something that would not have society perform that most terrible of all acts and yet would give them some real assurance of an effective deterrent for this most terrible of all crimes. What we offered and what was passed as an alternative is a frightening imposition on any human being, no matter how terrible that human being is. To lock someone up for life, it has been argued in this House, is worse than having the state destroy them because, indeed, if you are incarcerated for life, what is human life? I only argue that we had an obligation to give the public some protection.
In the course of giving that very severe deterrent, 25 years before consideration of parole, with that "glimmer of hope" clause, we have in fact left ourselves as a parliament free to consider any revision or change in that, when parliament itself or those people who are concerned about the extremity of the penalty-and we all should be because that penalty is most extreme-can prove that that is not necessary and that we can protect ourselves and provide sufficient deterrent then, indeed, we can change the law from its present, very severe form.
The issue of deterrent is always the basic argument on the question of the death penalty. I had an opportunity to freshen my mind considerably on this subject a couple of days ago, along with a colleague of mine on this side of the House, a colleague from the other side of the House, a chaplain who in fact witnessed the last hangings at the Don jail, and a man for whom I have the greatest respect, the chief of police of metropolitan Toronto, Mr. Harold Adamson, when 1 taped a program for the Global Television Network. In the course of that debate-and I do not think that I am being unfair to my colleagues who attended, but they of course can review Hansard-I must say that when pressed it is impossible for either side to prove that the death penalty is or is not a deterrent. If anybody watches that program, and if I can plug it, it is running tomorrow night from nine o'clock to ten o'clock, they will find, and it was agreed, that it simply cannot be proved. Chief Adamson agreed with this position.
The hon. member opposite who preceded me said that people must have a fear of death and that nobody could tell him that it would not work. I believe that that is an emotional argument. The fact of the matter is that in 1889 Rhode Island abolished the death penalty, and Rhode Island has a lower murder rate than adjacent states which have had the death penalty for many more years. In California several years ago they took a referendum on the death penalty, the result of which indicated that people were overwhelmingly in favour of the death penalty, but in the months that followed, the murder rate in California soared. One would think that potential murderers, seeing that the death penalty is coming back, would fear that, but that is not the case. I am simply saying that the deterence argument is neither valid for me as an abolitionist nor for the retentionists. It cannot be proven. And

March 2, 1979
Criminal Code
if it cannot be proven, then surely we should not, as a state, be taking human life.
I also had an opportunity to discuss this matter at a national convention of my party about three years ago. I am proud to say that at that convention my party voted, albeit by a very narrow vote, for abolition of the death penalty, but at the same time said, "We want tougher laws to deal with the broad range of murder where in fact they could be paroled in six, seven or eight years, and now in fact face 25 years". At that particular session I described how, if I personally suffered the murder of someone close to me, such as my wife or a member of my family, that I could not imagine any other reaction within me than a desire either personally or to have the state not only erradicate that person but probably torture the individual and stretch him from limb to limb. But, again, we are human beings, and we have our own emotions and concerns. Therefore, I would not expect any other reaction from the most sensitive of human beings, and I do not claim to be that. What I am saying is that the state must represent a higher order than each of us as individuals could represent at a particular moment of duress or concern.
Over the years the issue of the death penalty has prompted many police officers and organizations of policemen to come forward and lobby politicians to reinstate the death penalty or, when it was in existence to make the death penalty more severe. I would like to refer to some comments I made in a speech on this subject in 1976, as they are reported in Hansard at page 13244.
I have the greatest respect for Canadian police forces, for the RCMP, and certainly for the police force in my own area of metropolitan Toronto, but in all fairness it should be pointed out that police officers and prison guards go into their work knowing the risks they face and they are trained to be prepared for those risks. I am arguing that the law as it is now constituted simply does not seem to be fair. If we investigate statistics of the average of fatalities on the job for 10,000 employees in Canada from 1964 to 1973, the highest on the job fatality rate is for miners. The second highest is for loggers, then fishermen, transport workers, labourers, and police officers rank sixth.
If we consider the jeopardy of these fine men and women police officers who protect us, if we can stand back from the emotion and look at the situation objectively, we must admit that the risk of losing life in their work is less than for many other people in our society.
I shall not go at great length, Mr. Speaker, because several other members want to discuss this problem. There are two other areas I should like to touch on, however. First is the record of the rate of murder in Canada in recent years. In 1974 the murder rate per 100,000 people was 2.4; in 1975, 2.8; 1976, 2.7; and in 1977, 2.7. The death penalty was abolished in 1976, but the murder rate remained the same the following year, and in 1976-77 it was marginally less than in 1975. In 1974, it was lower than in the following three years. Surely that suggests that the death penalty does not have a direct effect as a deterrent.
The second thing I wanted to deal with is the statistics which suggest that in recent years in Canada 86 to 90 per cent of violent crime is armed assault, and assault. Of the 86 per

cent of violent crime, murder represents only a small percentage point. I suppose we can never really say "only", because taking human life by murder is extreme, and that is why I am an abolitionist.
The public, not having had the time or opportunity to look into this issue thoughtfully, and learning about violence in our society, believes that the death penalty is the fast answer to their fears about their well-being and the state of our society. I do not believe the general public even knew, when we had the death penalty, who could be hanged and for what crimes.
The old provision of the death penalty for the killers of police and prison guards on duty, was not a protection for them at all. Very few were murdered, but for some there was a great danger of assault. In 1976 a parallel bill was passed which strongly toughened the penalties for the lesser and more numerous crimes of assault.
It might help if we could take the Canadian public, group by group-and I am not being condescending but rather pointing out that it is our job to be thoughtful about an issue and do what we think is responsible and effective as I believe we did with the bill in 1976-and explained that the laws are tougher, and more convictions are being obtained for the broader range of violent crime.
I think I shall leave it at that, Mr. Speaker, except to argue that I will be saddened indeed if this issue is not discussed objectively in the coming election campaign. We have a responsibility, no matter what party we belong to, when affairs of government are so confusing and life has so much tension, to explain the issues to people, with intelligence and knowledge.
Sir Robert Mark, the former superintendent of Scotland Yard in Great Britain, said he was not terribly concerned about whether Great Britain executed people or not. He said he had a great deal of difficulty getting convictions because in this modern society, where there is real concern about taking human life, juries disagree. As a result, the accused is often incarcerated on a manslaughter charge or convicted of second degree murder with a sentence of six or seven years. He said that he would like to see the death penalty abolished and tough sentencing substituted so that they could get criminals off the streets.
With my reservations about the severity of penalties, that is the kind of broadly effective law that we have had for several years. It would be very sad indeed if this House were to change its position today, because there is wide misunderstanding on the issue and because the bill looks like a quick and easy answer to the concerns of the public.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to be able to enter this debate today. I missed the debate in 1976, but I took part in the 1973 debate on the side of abolition. I think the suggestion that there was not a free expression of opinion in those debates is not correct. It was insisted in our caucus that everyone should vote according to his or her conscience.
March 2, 1979

It is correct to say that the death penalty is not a deterrent. This has been amply demonstrated in many surveys. A large prison near Detroit has probably more murderers on death row than any other prison in the world, and it is obvious that none of them would be deterred from repeating the crime by threat of death. Speaking as a doctor, I believe that a murderer has a unique personality. That is not to say that all of the potential murderers are in jail-there may be some here in the House of Commons who would like to do murder once in a while!
We should realize that people who will commit murder are not deterred by the fear of their own death. Murder is an action they take on their way to a certain goal, or it is the goal itself and nothing is going to deter them from the deed. If we realize that, we should also realize that all our finer feelings of civilization are wasted when we consider the role of the murderer except to say that if we take life, no matter whether by hanging or in any other way, we are causing death. This is rather an antithesis to our ideas of civilization. We must apprehend the criminal who has committed murder and make sure he is not released into society again. I believe in recidivism. The idea that people who have committed murder can be prevented from doing it again is an entirely wrong premise. Murderers are unique in psychological type. When sent to prison they act like model Sunday school boys. Murderers have attained their goal, so why must they act in any other way? Given the same set of circumstances, when released from jail, the whole psychological mechanism will be set in motion again and the cycle will be repeated.
As far as collective conscience is concerned, a point entered by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), one cannot depend on that. Socrates advocated new knowledge, and collective conscience had him drink the hemlock. Our own religion was against the collective conscience of that day. Tyranny has always put down collective conscience. We had such things as the inquisition, and following that the reformation. It seems to me that one cannot depend on the emotional ideas and decisions of a people of a certain time in the world's history as being collectively correct, no matter whether it is acceptable to the majority or not. In that sense majority does not mean a great deal.
In my opinion parole for a killer is wrong. I do not believe that a murderer, because he has acted as a fine individual in prison for ten or 15 years, ought to be let out. I would not think of letting him out. In my view the only solution is to keep him in prison until he is harmless. The 25-year idea of imprisonment is fairly good, but not perfect. One must realize that the death penalty is not a deterrent. After the criminal is in prison one must make sure that he is not released. If he acts well in prison and performs some kind of useful work, he might have some degree of personal satisfaction. For instance, a criminal might be satisfied that he can make amends for what he has done. It seems to me this would give him some hope for life and maybe for the next life. I do not believe that release from prison is the solution.
Criminal Code
It is very important that we do not subscribe to capital punishment as revenge or as a deterrent. Instead, these people must be taken away from society. But let them try to carry on some kind of life in prison or by doing some work that is satisfying to them, during which time they might make some atonement.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention will be short. I rise to support Bill C-29 introduced by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga).
I would like to say that the wishes of the Canadian people should be expressed in this House especially when such a large number of people are in favour of capital punishment. Polls that have been taken reflect this opinion vividly. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming) said the public have not had time to look into this subject objectively. I do not believe it. I do not believe the public at large would buy that statement. This subject has been to the forefront during our lifetime. People have watched closely the progress of the various bills presented in this House over the years. They have followed this subject more closely than any other. They very well know what happens to people on parole and to people serving life sentences. They have seen these things and they know exactly what is going on.
The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) stated that the last vote on capital punishment in the House of Commons reflected a true cross-section of opinion. I wish it were the case that we could have a true vote in this House of Commons. I almost believed it would happen until I saw what went on in the last few days before the vote took place. I realize it is very difficult to obtain a true vote in this House when a bill is introduced. When it is a government bill it is put forward in the name of the government. We know immediately that there is cabinet solidarity. Cabinet solidarity showed up in the last vote taken on capital punishment.
In my opinion the only way one can have a free vote in this House is to have a vote on a private member's bill. Since it is not a government bill, cabinet solidarity is not needed and there are no pressures put on members, as has been the case in the past. Under the existing rules I realize we will not get far when it comes to having a vote on a private member's bill. The government will not let it go through. The government knows that all it must do is to sit for an hour and talk out a private member's bill so as to avoid having to do anything about it. Occasionally a private member's bill resolution goes through. I have had a resolution passed; it was so embarrassing to the government that they allowed it, but it was all more or less pre-arranged beforehand.
There should be some changes in the rules in order to give precedence and more weight to private members' bills. I am not just talking about a debate on capital punishment. A lot of good bills presented to this House by private members never get the full discussion or the precedence they deserve. I know it is embarrassing to government members to have to stand up and talk these private members' bills out, because very often they believe they are good and deserving of more emphasis than is given.

March 2, 1979
Criminal Code
It would be much better, in my view, if some other rules could be devised to cover private members' hour. As things are, not many members take the trouble to attend because they know bills will be talked out in any event and that they will not be called upon to make a decision. I think it would be much better if we were to adopt a system as is followed in the United States where a private member's bill means something to its sponsor, to his constituents, and to the people.
The subject now under discussion is of importance to the people of Canada. My own experience is that since the last vote on capital punishment was taken in the House, public opinion has hardened on the issue. I would have thought that a decision having been made, people would have softened their attitude. But this has not happened. For instance, only a few weeks ago a radio station in my riding put out an editorial on capital punishment, fairly early in the morning. Then the phone lines were opened and listeners were invited to say whether or not they favoured capital punishment. The lines were open for about half an hour and the station received 110 calls in that time. This shows how important people feel the subject to be. Over 90 per cent of those calls was in favour of capital punishment. That has been my experience, too. Public opinion has hardened, and I believe it is time this subject was raised by way of a private member's bill. Maybe the government will allow the issue to be decided in this way once and for all.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few points. The hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) introducing this bill, said it would bring back the death sentence only in cases of treason and premeditated murder. However, the explanatory notes to the bill talk about its purpose being to impose the death sentence in all cases of murder.
Along with the hon. member who has just spoken, he made the point that the vote which took place in this House three years or so ago on the subject was not a free vote. I think it is about time all of us in this House, and anybody in this country who is left to doubt, ought to admit that this was a free vote. It was a free vote by all members of parliament standing up on their own initiative and voting yes and no as they felt fit, and as their consciences dictated. That point bothered me a little because I have heard comments of that kind before from Conservative members. They try to label the vote which took place as being other than a free vote.
Let me point this out to the hon. member for Pembina. My hon. friend from Bruce-Grey, who has since become a parliamentary secretary, voted at that time to retain the death penalty. I, who last year served with the minister of justice who succeeded the minister of justice who presented that bill, voted retentionist. But it did not prevent either of us from becoming parliamentary secretaries. My hon. friend from St. Catharines, who also serves as a parliamentary secretary, voted with us. Some of the other parliamentary secretaries voted for abolition. They voted as free men with free con-

sciences, with no one in this party dictating to them or twisting their arms, or trying to put pressure on them in any way. Let us settle that question once and for all. We can go back, in our individual ways, and explain the stand we took to our electors if the matter comes up in the campaign. Let us not try to make a party political statement out of something which did not occur in this House.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think the last statement made by the hon. member has as much validity as his first statement with regard to my bill. It is obvious he has read only the first sentence and none of the clauses which define the offences in respect of which we hope to reinstate capital punishment, that is, high treason and premeditated murder. It is obvious the hon. gentleman is confused on that issue as well as on the issue of whether there was a free vote on that side of the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am not making statements and generalities, Mr. Speaker. I think I have proven my point. I have given examples, not only in my case but in the case of other members on this side. I might mention the hon. member for Skeena who is now a member of the cabinet who happened to vote in part the way I and some of my colleagues voted. I wonder where the members on that side of the House are this evening who voted abolitionist at that time and could be here in private members' hour today. Is this some kind of little game among members of the Conservative party? We know the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has consented to allow a private member to bring on a bill to reintroduce capital punishment, without making any hard and fast rules on it, but are there some members over there who want to speak according to their consciences?
I can answer the hon. member's question very quickly by saying yes, if he would allow me time in which to do so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would be very glad to leave the hon. member some time to speak on the bill this afternoon. I heard comments during this discussion to the effect that the will of the Canadian people was not allowed to be carried out as a result of the vote which took place. The hon. member for Pembina says that according to a Gallup poll between 80 and 85 per cent of the Canadian public felt that the death penalty should be enforced. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that the figures are 80 per cent or 85 per cent in favour of the death penalty. I have done some research in my own constituency, and 1 would be inclined to say they run somewhere in the order of 65 per cent in favour and 35 per cent opposed, but even then there are uncertainties expressed when people are asked what they really mean.
I sent out a newsletter at the time, balancing the arguments for and against the death penalty, and I invited my constituents to write to me on the subject. Of some 35,000 polled households in my riding which received the newsletter 1 got back some 700 responses. I read each of those responses several times. I read them the day they came in, I read them
March 2, 1979

during the course of the debate on capital punishment, on Bill C-84, the evening before I voted, and again before I voted in the morning. It was clear to me that even those who were very strong retentionists were saying that they did not really believe in capital punishment for all cases of murder, except in cases of premeditated murder.
People felt very strongly about the murder of policemen and prison guards on duty, and I shared some of those feelings. People in this country were telling me that they felt very strongly about others being killed through bombings, terrorism and hijacking. I lived in Europe a few years ago. I studied and travelled there. A couple of terrorist bombs exploded in a neighbourhood relatively close to where I was living. At one time windows in the little apartment in which I lived were shattered. I shared some of that concern. I do not want to get into explaining why or how I voted the way I did at the time, but those were some of the thoughts which were going through my mind.
We are asked this afternoon to consider Bill C-219, legislation to amend the Criminal Code with respect to the death sentence. The bill provides for mandatory death sentences in all cases of murder, and restricts the traditional authority of the governor in council to commute such sentences to cases where a jury or a majority of a jury makes a positive recommendation for clemency.
The bill also reintroduces some former provisions of the Criminal Code, such as postponements of executions of pregnant women until at least a few days after they have delivered their children, forbidding executions of those under 18 years of age, rights of appeal, methods of procedures for executions- which I note would be hanging-places of burial of executed persons, and so forth. It pains me somewhat to think that we would return to thoughts of executing a woman who had just given birth to a child and orphaning that child.
It may be said that this bill would turn the clock back to the situation which prevailed prior to 1960. It would turn the clock back to a situation which prevailed before the amendments which were brought in by the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, then minister of justice in a cabinet led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). I think that was in 1961. Those amendments introduced a differentiation between premeditated murder and non-premeditated murder. We now have first degree and second degree classifications.
Today we are debating, for the fifth time in 13 years, the issue of capital punishment. What this bill would do would be to dismiss the decision taken by this House just about three years ago when I think almost half the members of the House individually participated freely in that debate, and when the House voted freely.
I know that one of my hon. colleagues opposite wants to speak. I will perhaps just summarize. All first and second degree murder cases, given the passage of this bill, would attract a mandatory sentence of death by hanging in the event of conviction, not only of those individuals found guilty of
Criminal Code
planned and deliberate murder, the murder of a police officer or prison guard or murder committed in the course of committing certain other crimes, but also those individuals convicted for spur of the moment crimes, crimes of passion, which have troubled many people, even the most ardent retentionists, for a long time.
One of the difficulties with this bill is the issue of leaving it to a jury to make a recommendation to the governor in council. The way it is drafted, this bill would require a judge to poll the jury on whether its members might make a recommendation for clemency or no recommendation. However, it does not give a jury any guidelines. It does not give any instructions to the judge for when he is instructing the jury. What would happen if jurors wish to remain silent? What would happen in the case of a 12-person jury in which four or five wish to recommend clemency and the other seven or eight are unable to make a recommendation? The bill says nothing about jurors wishing to remain silent.
I know from my practice of law over a limited period of time that when we had the death sentence for murder it was very difficult in many cases to get convictions, simply because juries were loath to think of the person on trial before them actually being disposed of by hanging. Juries could not face that in their minds, so they often convicted people of lesser crimes than first degree or premeditated murder.
I could go on and make a number of other comments. I have pushed the clock along somewhat more than I wished. I did want to leave my hon. colleague opposite some time in which to make comments, and I think I will stop at this point.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the generosity of the hon. member opposite, who has left me all of two minutes for what may well be the last speech I will have a chance to give in this chamber, which I will be leaving.
It was the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Okanagan-Boundary (Mr. Whittaker), which moved me to speak. He will be returned to this House, and he needs no assistance from me in the coming election campaign on this subject, but being a member of generous heart I am prepared to offer him a little assistance because I know he was serious when he spoke in favour of and demanded a free vote in parliament. That means freeing members from party discipline and freeing them to vote according to their conscience on the issue at hand.
I also listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga), who asked how a member such as myself could pit my conscience against public opinion on the cause to which he and the hon. member for Okanagan-Boundary referred. It is quite easy, because there is another test of the common sense of the public and that, of course, is in the decisions of juries in jury trials. I keep track of these. A jury at Kamloops, British Columbia, reduced the charge against the murderer of Patrick Charles Danchuk. The charge was reduced to manslaughter, and the accused was sentenced to four years. That is a test of the common sense of the public.

March 2, 1979
Criminal Code
It is a truer test than the amateurish polls which are taken from time to time, because when 12 good people and true get together they express the public opinion. I suspect, had we returned to capital punishment, the jury in that case would have acquitted, as the jury would have acquitted in the case of Maxwell, who was murdered in Kelowna. There was a reduced charge also, through plea bargaining, of the murderer of Sadie Jones Edward at Sicamous, British Columbia. One can follow these cases. That is the true test.
I hope this parliament will not ever return this nation to capital punishment. I admired the courage of one Lowell Green for suggesting in the Ottawa Journal that in the future, if there are to be executions, they be televised publicly. I see no reason why they should not. We have allowed the monster of television into this chamber, and I do not know how we can
keep it out of anything else it might be interested in getting into, including the courts. If this chamber, the highest court of the land, is televised, then every other court of the land should be televised so that the public can watch the process of justice, particularly in cases of murder. Then I think we would have justification for the vote which was taken in this House.
One notes, of course, that the murder rate dropped after the decision to abolish capital punishment. I believe we saved some lives, and not just those of murderers.
